reports.summary: A VU9P can comfortably host DEFLATE compression at the project's required 3-6 GB/s (25-50 Gbps) alongside a NIC shell: AMD's Vitis Data Compression Library delivers 2 GB/s per gzip/zlib kernel WITH dynamic Huffman (~54-60K LUTs, ~130-141 BRAM, 64 URAM per kernel at ~300 MHz on Alveo U200, which is VU9P-class silicon), so 2-3 kernels reach 4-6 GB/s for under ~15% of the VU9P's 1.18M LUTs; single-engine static-Huffman designs (Ledwon HLS: 4.0 GB/s at 250 MHz, 69K LUTs, 260 BRAM; Fowers/Microsoft FCCM'15: 5.6 GB/s at 175 MHz, ~100-108K ALMs) prove one engine alone can cover the whole profitable region, and Corundum's measured VCU118 footprint (62.4K LUTs = 5%, 331 BRAM = 15%, 20 URAM at 100G) confirms NIC-shell coexistence with >70% of the device left over. The ratio penalty is the key risk: hardware dynamic-Huffman deflate (Vitis, 32KB blocks) achieves 2.70 on Silesia vs software zlib -6 at 3.107 (-13%), while hardware-friendly static-Huffman variants pay much more (Vitis fixed: 2.31, -26%; Fowers: 2.09 and Ledwon: 1.92 on Calgary vs ~2.6-2.7 for zlib, i.e. -20 to -27%) — and because WR-ZipGuard's entire wire saving is only ~27-30% (alpha 0.70-0.73), even a 13% ratio penalty could roughly halve the saving, so the alpha numbers MUST be re-measured under hardware constraints (zlib Z_FIXED strategy emulates static Huffman in software for free) before committing an architecture. ASIC references bracket the design space: Microsoft Corsica does 100 Gbps compress+encrypt (Zipline RTL is open-sourced on OCP GitHub), Intel QAT gen4 lists 160 Gbps verified compression per socket, measured Intel IAA does 0.99 GB/s compress / 3.83 GB/s decompress per synchronous job at ratio 2.55 vs 3.32 for software deflate, and CAST's ZipAccel-C commercial IP claims >100 Gbps feasible in FPGAs. The byte-transpose/channel-major forward transform is cheap in logic (fixed permutation: w-bank RAM + two switch networks per Püschel/Milder/Hoe JACM'09) but needs on-chip buffering >= one reorder chunk (Garrido TCAS-I 2020 proves M >= N words for continuous flow), i.e. ~2-4 MB of URAM for the project's 2MB chunks — about 6-12% of the VU9P's 33.75 MB URAM — so the transform is a buffering problem, not a logic problem.

# FPGA DEFLATE Compression Survey (encode side) — for WR-ZipGuard VCU118/VU9P pivot

## 0. VU9P budget baseline (VCU118 = XCVU9P)
Device totals (AMD datasheet, standard figures): **1,182,240 LUTs; 2,364,480 FFs; 2,160 BRAM36 (75.9 Mb = 9.49 MB); 960 URAM (270 Mb = 33.75 MB); 6,840 DSP48E2**. Alveo U200 = same VU9P-class silicon, so Vitis U200 benchmark numbers transfer almost directly to VCU118 (VCU118 ships a -2 speed grade; Vitis kernels close at ~300 MHz).

## 1. AMD Vitis Data Compression Library (primary vendor source)
Benchmarked on **Alveo U200**, Silesia corpus, from the official benchmark pages (2021.1 and 2022.1 essentially identical):

| Kernel | Block | Ratio | Throughput | FMax | LUT | BRAM | URAM |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GZip/Zlib MM (dyn. Huffman) | 32KB | **2.70** | **2 GB/s** | 300MHz | 57-60K | 135 | 64 |
| GZip/Zlib Stream (dyn.) | 32KB | 2.70 | 2 GB/s | 293-300MHz | 54K | 128-141 | 64 |
| **GZip Fixed (static Huffman)** | 32KB | **2.31** | 2 GB/s | 300MHz | **35K** | **43-45** | 64 |
| Zlib Fixed | 32KB | 2.31 | 2 GB/s | 300MHz | 35.7K | 39 | 64 |
| GZip Stream 8KB blocks | 8KB | 2.50 | 2 GB/s | 300MHz | 57.5K | 100 | 48 |
| Zstd quad-core (reference) | 32KB | 2.68 | 1.17 GB/s | 283MHz | 40K | 80 | 37 |
| (decode side, for context) GZip/Zlib decompress | — | — | 518 MB/s | 273-283MHz | 6.7-6.9K | 8 | 0 |

Key facts:
- Each 2 GB/s "kernel" is internally a multi-core (8-engine) design over 32KB blocks; output is a **standard deflate/zlib/gzip stream** ("Dynamic Huffman, Fixed Huffman and Stored Blocks" all supported) — i.e., BF3-decodable single stream, matching the project's C2 constraint.
- AMD states 19.3x speedup of one gzip compress kernel vs single-core zlib-fast, and that U200 has "room for more compute units" — multi-CU scaling is the intended path.
- **Cost of dynamic vs static in hardware at equal 2 GB/s**: dynamic costs ~+20K LUTs and ~+90 BRAM per kernel but buys ratio 2.70 vs 2.31 (+17%).
- **Ratio vs software**: zlib -6 on Silesia = 32.19% compressed size = ratio **3.107** (lzbench, zlib 1.3.1, EPYC 9554); zlib -1 = 36.45% = 2.743. So Vitis dynamic-Huffman HW pays **-13% vs zlib -6** (2.70/3.107), roughly matching zlib -1; fixed-Huffman HW pays **-26%**.

## 2. Academic / open FPGA deflate encoders (compression side)

Consolidated comparison (Ledwon thesis Table 3.3 + primary papers):

| Design | Year | Device | Clock | B/cyc | Throughput | Ratio (Calgary) | Area |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| IBM (Martin et al., ICCAD'13) | 2013 | Altera Stratix V | 200MHz | 16 | 3.0 GB/s | 2.17 | ~105.6K ALMs, 1,152 M20K |
| Altera/Abdelfattah "Gzip on a chip" (IWOCL'14, OpenCL) | 2014 | Stratix-V A7 | 193MHz | 16 | 2.84 GB/s | 2.17 (2.43 Canterbury) | 47% logic, 70% RAM of A7 (~110K ALMs, 1,792 M20K) |
| **Fowers et al. (Microsoft, FCCM'15), static Huffman** | 2015 | Stratix V | 175MHz | 8/16/24/32 | 1.4 / 2.8 / 4.2 / **5.6 GB/s** | 1.82 / 2.05 / 2.09 / 2.09 (w/ head-tail) | 16.5K / 39.1K / 68.6K / **108.4K ALMs** |
| Qiao (UCLA FCCM'18, HARP CPU-FPGA) | 2018 | Arria 10 | 200MHz | 16 | 2.8 GB/s/engine; 3.9-10 GB/s multi-way end-to-end | ~2.0-2.1 | 83.6K LUTs, 65K FFs per engine |
| **Ledwon/Cockburn/Han (IEEE Access 2020, Vivado HLS), static Huffman** | 2020 | **XCVU3P** (Virtex US+) | **250MHz** | 16 | **4.0 GB/s** | **1.92 geo / 2.00 arith** | **69,114 LUTs (17.5% VU3P = ~5.8% VU9P), 49,779 FFs, 260.5 BRAM (36% VU3P = ~12% VU9P)**; LZ77 encoder alone 62.2K LUTs/240 BRAM, Huffman encoder 6.9K LUTs/20.5 BRAM; 49 pipeline stages |
| MetaZip (DAC'22) | 2022 | FPGA (CPU-attached) | — | adaptive, up to 64 | **15.6 GB/s single engine** (2.78x prior FPGA best) | balanced via MetaHistory/Seed-Bypass/Serialization-Predictor submodules | not in abstract |
| hdl-deflate (OpenCores, open HDL) | — | generic | — | ~0.5 | ~1 byte per 2 cycles (FAST option: whole-window match/cycle) | — | small |

Fowers FCCM'15 full Table I (Calgary corpus) — the canonical throughput/ratio/area frontier:
- ZLIB (fastest sw) 0.038 GB/s, ratio 2.62
- PWS=8: 1.4 GB/s, 1.74 (1.82 w/ head-tail), 14.5K (16.5K) ALMs
- PWS=16: 2.8 GB/s, 1.93 (2.05), 35.1K (39.1K) ALMs
- PWS=24: 4.2 GB/s, 1.97 (2.09), 63.9K (68.6K) ALMs
- PWS=32: 5.6 GB/s, 1.97 (2.09), 100.8K (108.4K) ALMs
- Architecture: 64K-entry hash, **HBN=32 banks with conflict-dropping** (bank conflicts dropped after 2nd request — pipeline never stalls, costs ratio), hash-table-depth HTD=1 (multi-table design replaces head/prev chains), 64KB data window replicated PWS times for parallel match, match-trim vs head/tail selection (**match trimming alone loses 10-20% ratio; head/tail reduces loss to 2-6%**), fully pipelined 22+2*PWS+log2(PWS) stages, static Huffman + barrel-shifter bit-packers. Area scales quadratically in PWS for data memory + match selection → array-of-small-engines is the resource-efficient way to hit a target GB/s (their Fig. 9: a PWS=32 engine buys +15% ratio over 4x PWS=8 engines for +64% area).
- "Gzip on a chip" details: VEC=16 parallel dictionaries, 10-bit hash of 4 bytes (hash function choice worth ~7% absolute ratio), last-fit bin-packing match filter with reach optimization (+8% ratio), II=1 at 193 MHz.

## 3. ASIC line-rate references (calibration points, all deflate-family)
- **Microsoft Project Zipline / Corsica** (Broadcom co-designed ASIC): **100 Gbps compression+encryption in-line**, XP10 format (LZ77+Huffman family, >20% better ratio than "Zlib-L4 64KB" on cloud data). **Full RTL open-sourced** in OCP GitHub repo (rtl/, dv/ for CCE_64/CDD_64/KME engines, syn/ scripts; 76% SystemVerilog) — sized for ASIC, no FPGA throughput/area numbers published.
- **Intel QAT gen4 (Sapphire Rapids)**: "200 Gbps crypto and **160 Gbps verified compression**" per socket (up to 4 QAT endpoints); measured real-world ~73 Gb/s using 1.6 cores.
- **Intel IAA (on-die, Sapphire Rapids), measured by CMU (ADMS'25/VLDB workshop, DuckDB/TPC-H)**: Deflate IAA **compress 0.99 GB/s, decompress 3.83 GB/s** per synchronous job stream, **ratio 2.55 vs 3.32 for software Deflate CPU** (IAA supports only one compression level; 4 IAA devices x 8 Acceleration Engines on the test machine; 4 GB max single job). Dynamic Huffman on IAA requires a **two-pass** flow (statistics pass + encode pass); "canned"/fixed single-pass modes trade ratio for latency — a clean documented instance of the static-vs-dynamic hardware tradeoff.
- **IBM zEDC → z15 NXU**: on-chip nest accelerator for DEFLATE; IBM claims up to 8x faster elapsed time vs z14 zEDC Express PCIe card and "order of magnitude" throughput increase moving on-chip; no public GB/s spec found.
- **AHA3642** (from IWOCL'14 comparison): 20 Gbit/s deflate ASIC at ratio 3.6 (Canterbury) — shows dedicated ASICs with big ratio use much deeper search than any line-rate FPGA design.
- **CAST ZipAccel-C** (commercial IP, System Verilog): ">100 Gbps feasible in FPGAs", >400 Gbps at 500 MHz in ASIC, <100 KGates minimum footprint, latency down to tens of cycles, scales by instantiating more search engines/Huffman encoders; available for Alveo. (Marketing numbers; no per-config ratio disclosed.)

## 4. Static vs dynamic Huffman: hardware tradeoff quantified
- Equal-throughput, same library (Vitis, Silesia): dynamic 2.70 vs fixed 2.31 → **static pays -14.4% ratio**, but saves ~35% LUTs and ~70% BRAM of the kernel.
- vs software zlib -6 (Silesia 3.107): HW dynamic -13%, HW static -26%.
- High-throughput academic designs almost all choose **static** Huffman (Fowers, Ledwon, Qiao) because true dynamic needs two passes (or block-buffered tree-gen) — Vitis solves it with per-32KB-block tree generation inside the pipeline; Abdelfattah computed the tree on the host and refreshed it occasionally (deployment-static, data-adaptive).
- **Critical caveat for WR-ZipGuard**: all corpus penalties above are text-like data. The project's alpha=0.70-0.73 leaves only 27-30% wire saving; scaling the Vitis -13% ratio penalty onto ratio 1.37 gives ratio ~1.19 (alpha ~0.84) — i.e., **a corpus-typical hardware penalty would cut the saving roughly in half and push B_crit further down**. Because the transformed-KV win lives almost entirely in the exponent plane (skewed byte histogram → Huffman-sensitive), static-vs-dynamic penalty on THIS data is unknown and cheaply measurable in software: **zlib's Z_FIXED strategy emulates static-Huffman deflate; limited-depth hash / greedy (Z_FAST-like) settings bound the LZ77-simplification penalty**. This should be the first pre-FPGA experiment, and it keeps the BF3-decodability invariant (Z_FIXED output is still standard deflate).

## 5. LZ77 match-engine parallelization on FPGA (mechanism summary)
Standard recipe (IBM'13 / Altera'14 / Fowers'15 / Vitis all variants of it): process W bytes/cycle; W parallel hash lookups into **multi-banked, multi-table hash dictionaries** (bank conflicts dropped, not stalled — costs ratio, keeps II=1); W parallel byte-comparators against candidate windows; match-selection stage resolves overlaps (combinational reduction [Altera] / pipelined trim+head-tail [Fowers] / bin-packing last-fit with reach [Abdelfattah, +8% ratio]); static-Huffman encode + barrel-shifter bit-packing. Known costs: conflict-dropping + window-trimming are exactly where the 10-25% ratio loss vs software zlib comes from; deeper hash tables (HTD>=2) claw some back. MetaZip (DAC'22) pushes to 64B/cycle (15.6 GB/s) with adaptive-width pipeline. For the 3-6 GB/s target, W=16 at 250 MHz (Ledwon, on Virtex US+ like VU9P) is already proven in HLS — no exotic microarchitecture needed.

## 6. Byte-transpose / channel-major reorder engines on FPGA
- Both transforms are **fixed permutations**, so the canonical result applies: Püschel/Milder/Hoe, "Permuting streaming data using RAMs" (JACM 56(2), 2009; US Patent 8,321,823): a streaming width-w permutation needs **w independent RAM banks (total capacity N words), plus two w-port switching networks**, running at full throughput; the paper gives constructive algorithms and cost lower bounds for bit-linear permutations (stride/corner-turn/perfect-shuffle — the byte-transpose IS a stride permutation).
- Garrido & Pirsch, "Continuous-Flow Matrix Transposition Using Memories" (IEEE TCAS-I 67(9), 2020): continuous-flow transposition requires **memory M >= N** (N = elements per transposed block) and shows how to reach exactly N (vs 2N ping-pong) with read-before-write in-place addressing — an ISCAS-friendly citation.
- Henriksson & Gustafsson, "Streaming Matrix Transposition on FPGAs Using Distributed Memories" (IEEE NorCAS 2023): distributed-memory (LUTRAM) variants cheaper for small/medium matrices.
- **Cost estimate for WR-ZipGuard on VU9P**: logic is negligible (fixed wire permutation + w x w switches, O(w log w) muxes on a 64-byte AXI bus); the real cost is **buffering = the reorder scope**. bf16 byte-transpose with per-chunk-contiguous planes at 2MB chunks: 2 MB (in-place scheduling) to 4 MB (ping-pong) of URAM = **6-12% of the VU9P's 33.75 MB URAM**; at 256KB chunks: 0.75-1.5% — trivially affordable. Channel-major reorder keyed by head_dim is likewise a fixed stride permutation at chunk scope with the same M >= N bound (plus simple address generation); if chunk size ever exceeded on-chip memory, it becomes a DDR4 corner-turn costing 2x chunk DRAM traffic (VCU118 has two DDR4-2400 x64 channels ~19.2 GB/s each, so even DRAM-bounced transposition sustains >6 GB/s one direction). Note the forward transform on the sender FPGA composes trivially with the deflate engine as a streaming pre-stage; its area is dwarfed by the LZ77 hash/match memories.

## 7. Coexistence with a NIC shell on VU9P (measured anchor)
Corundum FCCM'20 (open-source 100G NIC, supports VCU118 out of the box) measured on **VCU118/XCVU9P, PCIe gen3 x16, 2x100G ports**: **62.4K LUTs (5%), 76.8K FFs (3%), 331 BRAM (15%), 20 URAM (2%)**, sustaining 78.7 Gbps with 16K MTU (10G config: 70.0K LUTs, 252 BRAM). Adding 2-3 Vitis dynamic-Huffman kernels (~110-180K LUTs, ~270-420 BRAM, 128-192 URAM) + a 4MB transform buffer (~120-135 URAM) totals roughly **20-25% LUTs, ~30% BRAM, ~20% URAM of the VU9P** — large margin for the RDMA/DMA glue, even before considering a leaner static-Huffman single engine.

## 8. Direct answers to the key questions
1. **Achievable compress throughput on VU9P beside a NIC shell**: 2 GB/s per Vitis kernel (dynamic Huffman, standard stream) with linear multi-CU scaling; 4.0 GB/s single-engine static-Huffman proven at 250 MHz on Virtex US+ (Ledwon, 69K LUTs); 5.6 GB/s single-engine (Fowers) and 15.6 GB/s (MetaZip) as upper references. The needed 3-6 GB/s is comfortably mid-range — roughly 10-20% of the device including the NIC — and does NOT require 100G-line-rate heroics.
2. **Ratio penalty vs zlib -6**: hardware dynamic-Huffman 32KB-block deflate: ~-13% (Silesia: 2.70 vs 3.107) ≈ zlib -1 territory; hardware static-Huffman high-throughput designs: -20% to -27% (Calgary: 1.92-2.17 vs ~2.6-2.74). On WR-ZipGuard's thin 27-30% saving this penalty is potentially fatal at the static end and material even at the dynamic end; must re-measure alpha under Z_FIXED + reduced-search constraints on real KV planes before choosing the hardware ratio/throughput point. The Vitis dynamic-Huffman path (13% corpus penalty, exact penalty on KV data unknown and plausibly smaller since the exponent-plane redundancy is short-range) at 2 GB/s/kernel is the safest starting point that preserves BF3 decodability.
3. **Resource budget**: deflate engine 35-69K LUTs + 40-260 BRAM + 0-64 URAM per 2-4 GB/s engine (3-6% of VU9P LUTs each); transform engine ~free in logic, 6-12% of URAM for 2MB-chunk buffering (scales linearly down with chunk size); NIC shell 5-6% LUTs / 15% BRAM (Corundum measured). Total system well under a third of the VU9P.

reports.summary: The user's 2026-10-13 deadline is exactly the ISCAS 2027 (Bordeaux, June 6-9, 2027) regular-paper deadline; notification is 2027-01-11. The page rule (per ISCAS 2025/2026 precedent, 2027 author instructions not yet posted) is stricter than "5 pages": maximum 5 pages of which only 4 may contain technical content (text + figures + references if any), with an optional 5th page for references ONLY; review is single-blind (ISCAS 2026 explicitly states "ISCAS is NOT double-blind review"), and CASS organizer guidelines target a flagship acceptance ratio "close to 45%". ISCAS has direct precedent for every ingredient of the pivoted paper: lossless compression of LLM float tensors with a hardware-friendly XOR/NOT transform (XNC, ISCAS 2025), a standard-codec (ZSTD/FSE) FPGA compression sub-block evaluated purely at module level on a Kintex-7 (ISCAS 2025), an RDMA NIC architecture paper (ScalaRNIC, ISCAS 2023), Tb/s P4 packet parsing on FPGA (ISCAS 2022), and FPGA LLM/transformer accelerators every year (UbiMoE, BETA, etc.). Evaluation norms at ISCAS are module-level: post-implementation resource tables (LUT/FF/BRAM/DSP), Fmax, throughput/latency, and a comparison table against 2-4 prior designs — no end-to-end two-node network demonstration is expected, and single-board/loopback or even synthesis-only evaluation is routinely accepted; live systems belong to a separate "Live Demonstrations" category. An accelerator-plus-measured-parameter analytical model fits ISCAS culture well provided the circuit is the centerpiece and the profitability frontier is compressed into roughly one figure plus one table; the nearest technical neighbor (LEXI, arXiv 2603.15589, exponent-entropy Huffman coding for inter-chiplet LLM traffic, 0.09% area overhead) confirms this "codec circuit + system latency model" template is the current style in circuits venues and is also the biggest novelty threat to cite and differentiate. Typical ISCAS contribution size is one well-executed idea (a transform + streaming engine + one killer measured number), which matches a VCU9P transform+deflate egress pipeline that meets ≥100 Gbps line rate and is decodable by commodity BlueField-3 hardware at the measured ~188 Gbps.

## 1. Venue rules: ISCAS 2027 is the target (deadline matches exactly)

### 1.1 Key dates (official ISCAS 2027 CFP, https://2027.ieee-iscas.org/call-for-papers)
| Item | Date |
|---|---|
| Special-session proposals | Sep 11, 2026 |
| **Regular papers / tutorials / live demos** | **Oct 13, 2026** |
| Author notification | Jan 11, 2027 |
| Final paper | Jan 27, 2027 |
| Conference | Jun 6-9, 2027, Bordeaux, France |

Note: ISCAS 2026's deadline was extended (to Oct 26, 2025), so a ~2-week extension is plausible but must not be planned on.

### 1.2 Page limit — stricter than "5 pages"
ISCAS 2027 author instructions are not yet posted; both ISCAS 2025 and ISCAS 2026 used the identical rule, quoted from the ISCAS 2026 author instructions (https://2026.ieee-iscas.org/authors/author-instructions.html) and ISCAS 2025 initial author instructions (https://2025.ieee-iscas.org/initial-author-instructions/):

> "Maximum 5 pages, of which 4 are for technical content including text, figures and references (if any), and with one additional optional 5th page containing only references"

So the real budget is **4 pages of technical content** (references may spill onto page 5 only). PDF, mandatory IEEE template, US Letter/A4, embedded fonts, 5 MB max; "Deviations from the above paper specifications could impede the review of your paper and result in rejection."

### 1.3 Review model
- ISCAS 2025: "Reviews will be single-blind." ISCAS 2026: "ISCAS is NOT double-blind review this year. Please include author information on your submission." Expect single-blind for 2027 (verify when author instructions post).
- No rebuttal stage appears anywhere in the official process pages; decision is one-shot (notification Jan 11, 2027). Reviewer count is not published (historically 2-3 reviews per paper; unverified from official sources).
- Selectivity: the 2025 CASS Guidelines for Conference Organizers state the acceptance ratio for the flagship conference (ISCAS) should be "close to 45%" excluding keynotes/special sessions (https://ieee-cas.org/files/ieeecass/2025-07/2025%20CASS%20Guidelines%20for%20Conference%20Organizers%20Form.pdf). So ISCAS is far less selective than FCCM/FPL — a competent, complete 4-page hardware paper with honest numbers has a good chance.

### 1.4 Relevant tracks (ISCAS 2027 CFP scope, 14 areas)
Best fits for the pivoted paper, exactly as named in the CFP:
- **Digital Integrated Circuits and Systems** (the natural home for an FPGA streaming datapath)
- **Communications Circuits and Systems** (NIC-path/inline-wire-data angle)
- **High-Performance Computing for AI** (new-ish area, LLM-serving angle — likely the most sympathetic reviewers for the KV-cache story)
- Neural Networks and Neuromorphic Engineering (accelerator papers also land here)
Other areas listed: Analog/Mixed-Signal, Power/Energy, Sensory, Nonlinear Systems and Circuit Theory, DSP, Multimedia, Biomedical, Quantum, Beyond-CMOS, Education.

Submission categories: Regular Papers ("original research contributions to the state-of-the-art in circuits and systems"), Special Sessions, Tutorials, and **Live Demonstrations** ("interactive demonstrations of working systems (hardware and/or software)") — a VCU118 loopback demo could be a low-cost companion submission. Selected papers are invited to journal extensions in IEEE CAS journals (TCAS-I/II path for the material that doesn't fit in 4 pages).

## 2. Concrete recent precedent papers (with one-line takeaways)

1. **XNC: XOR and NOT-Based Lossless Compression for Optimizing Unquantized Embedding Layers in Large Language Models — ISCAS 2025** (J. Lee et al., https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11043916/). *The single best precedent: a cheap bitwise transform (XOR adjacent 16-bit blocks + NOT) that makes LLM float tensors losslessly compressible, motivated by "embedding layers are sensitive to approximation, [so] lossless compression is more desirable than lossy" — exactly WR-ZipGuard's byte-transpose/channel-reorder-before-deflate shape, accepted at ISCAS with a 4-page budget.*
2. **A FPGA-based FSE Accelerator with Dynamic Table for ZSTD compression — ISCAS 2025** (Y. Lin, K. Liu, Z. Guo, https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11044267/). *A sub-block of a standard codec (FSE stage of ZSTD) on a Kintex-7 KC705 at 180 MHz, evaluated purely at module level — proves ISCAS accepts standard-compression-codec FPGA engines with no system deployment at all.*
3. **A Scalable RDMA Network Interface Card with Efficient Cache Management (ScalaRNIC) — ISCAS 2023** (X. Ma et al., https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10181426, DOI 10.1109/ISCAS46773.2023.10181426). *RDMA NIC microarchitecture (connection-cache management) is in-scope at ISCAS — direct precedent for NIC-path hardware without a full deployed network.*
4. **A Templated VHDL Architecture for Terabit/s P4-programmable FPGA-based Packet Parsing — ISCAS 2022** (P. Mashreghi-Moghadam et al.). *Network data-plane FPGA blocks judged on throughput/resource numbers are an established ISCAS genre.*
5. **UbiMoE: A Ubiquitous Mixture-of-Experts Vision Transformer Accelerator With Hybrid Computation Pattern on FPGA — ISCAS 2025** (J. Dong et al., arXiv:2502.05602, code released). *Typical strong ISCAS FPGA-accelerator paper: two kernel-level ideas + heuristic tuning, evaluated on ZCU102/U280 with 1.34x/3.55x throughput and 1.75x/1.54x energy-efficiency tables vs prior FPGA designs — that's the expected evaluation depth.*
6. **A High-Throughput Lossless Image Compression Engine Optimized for Compression Ratio — ISCAS 2024** (S. Cai et al.). *Lossless-compression engine papers with ratio+throughput tradeoff tables are a recurring ISCAS staple.*
7. **SLA hyperspectral on-board lossless compression on FPGA — ISCAS 2024, and its BIL-architecture variant — ISCAS 2025** (V. Joshi et al.). *ISCAS accepts incremental year-over-year follow-ups of the same compression engine — contribution granularity is genuinely small.*
8. **BETA: Binarized Energy-Efficient Transformer Accelerator at the Edge — ISCAS 2024** (Y. Ji et al.); plus ≥4 transformer-accelerator papers in each of ISCAS 2024/2025/2026 (SeVeDo 2026, sparse LLM accelerator 28nm 2026, spiking-transformer w/ KV product cache 2026, etc.). *LLM/transformer hardware is now a dense, welcomed topic at ISCAS.*
9. **LEXI: Lossless Exponent Coding for Efficient Inter-Chiplet Communication in Hybrid LLMs — arXiv 2603.15589 (Mar 2026, 7pp, venue pending)** (M. Sun, A. Kanani, K. Shroff, U. Ogras). *Closest technical neighbor and top must-cite/threat: observes "exponent streams exhibit fewer than 3 bits Shannon entropy," Huffman-codes bf16 exponents on inter-chiplet links, 33-45% link-latency reduction, 0.09% area/energy overhead @22nm — same exponent-plane physics as WR-ZipGuard, but chiplet-link scope, custom (non-standard) decoder, and no commodity-NIC decode constraint; differentiate on "one standard deflate stream decodable by commodity BF3 hardware at measured ~188 Gbps."*
10. **Corundum: An Open-Source 100-Gbps NIC — FCCM 2020** (A. Forencich et al., https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9114811/, https://github.com/corundum/corundum). *Practical enabler: mature open-source 100G FPGA NIC with a maintained VCU118 fpga_100g target (fpga/mqnic/VCU118/fpga_100g) — a credible shell for the loopback prototype; also proof that single-board NIC-platform evaluation is the community norm.*

Contextual extras: EBPC (Extended Bit-Plane Compression for DNN accelerators, arXiv:1908.11645, TCAS-I lineage) shows bit-plane transforms for tensor compression are an established CAS-community lineage; CERN HGCAL packet aggregator (ISCAS 2025) and RISC-V HyperSplit packet classification (ISCAS 2020) further confirm the networking-datapath genre.

## 3. What a competitive 5-page ISCAS paper looks like (synthesis)

**Contribution size.** One idea, executed end to end: a transform or codec trick + a streaming microarchitecture + one headline measured number. XNC is literally "two bitwise ops make LLM tensors compressible"; the ZSTD paper is "a dynamic-table FSE stage at 180 MHz." Multi-milestone systems papers (the full WR-ZipGuard M1-M4 arc) do NOT fit; the paper must be cut down to the sender-side transform+compress engine.

**Evaluation depth that is normal and accepted.**
- Post-implementation (or even post-synthesis) FPGA results: LUT/FF/BRAM/DSP table, Fmax, GB/s or Gbps throughput, latency cycles.
- Compression ratio tables on named datasets (for us: real captured KV from gpt2/Qwen2.5-7B/Llama-3.1-8B is *stronger* than the norm).
- A comparison table vs 2-4 prior designs (UbiMoE style: throughput x, energy-efficiency y vs SOTA).
- Single-board, loopback, or module-level testbench evaluation is standard; **no two-node network experiment is expected**. Nobody at ISCAS demonstrates end-to-end network bandwidth change; claiming "engine sustains >= line rate R while producing alpha=0.70 streams decodable by commodity BF3 hardware (measured 188 Gbps)" is exactly the right claim form.
- The absence of congestion-control signals is a non-issue at this venue: the gate can be presented as a policy input (threshold on measured bottleneck bandwidth), with the profitability frontier as the analytical justification.

**Does "circuit + measured-parameter analytical model" fit?** Yes, with the weight on the circuit. The accepted pattern is: Section II observation/transform (exponent-plane entropy, byte-transpose), Section III microarchitecture (streaming transform + deflate pipeline on XCVU9P), Section IV results (resources/Fmax/throughput/ratio + comparison), and the profitability frontier compressed to ~1 figure + ~4 lines of equations ("compression pays iff B < B_crit(alpha, X_comp, D_egress); with measured alpha=0.704 and BF3 D=188 Gbps, B_crit = 19-21 Gbps at 100G-FPGA sender"). LEXI (33-45% link-latency model on a chiplet system) shows codec-plus-system-model is the current style. What ISCAS will NOT reward: pages of methodology contracts, negative results, or model-only content with a thin circuit.

**Positioning risks.** (a) ISCAS reviewers are circuits people: lead with the datapath and Gbps/LUT numbers, not disaggregated-inference systems framing; keep the KV-cache/PD-disaggregation story to ~0.5 page of motivation. (b) LEXI and TRACE (IEEE TC, custom CXL silicon, alpha~0.53) must be cited and differentiated on the commodity-decodability constraint (one standard deflate stream, BF3-decodable) — that constraint is the paper's identity. (c) The 4-technical-page budget makes the M3/M1.5/M1.6 evidence base an asset only if ruthlessly summarized; consider a TCAS-II extension invitation as the vehicle for the full frontier analysis.

reports.summary: Strong, citable precedent exists for every one of the six single-board evaluation methodologies, including at top venues: SIGCOMM 2019 (PIEO) was accepted with zero external network traffic — per-flow packet generators synthesized on the FPGA itself plus on-chip token-bucket rate limiters swept from 0.1 to 32 Gbps to emulate link speeds; NSDI 2020 (Tonic) supported its 100 Gbps claim purely by FPGA synthesis/timing plus cycle-accurate simulation; OSDI 2021 (nanoPU) made a 69 ns wire-to-wire latency claim entirely inside FireSim cycle-accurate simulation; MICRO 2025 (NetZIP) kept its FPGA-NIC prototype to functional verification and payload-shrinking emulation while routing the 35% end-to-end headline through SimAI simulation. Dedicated FPGA-tester papers (Covington's NetFPGA packet generator FCCM 2009, OSNT IEEE Network 2014, FlueNT10G FPL 2018) legitimize trace replay from on-card DRAM with 6.25-6.4 ns hardware timestamping, and the FPGA compression-engine literature (FCCM 2011/2015/2018, IWOCL 2014) established host-PCIe-streaming as the standard way to measure engine throughput (2.66-12.8 GB/s measured this way). Port-to-port QSFP loopback on a single board and MAC/PCS near-end PMA loopback are vendor-documented methodologies (AMD AVED xbtest embedded packet generator + on-chip 48-bit MAC counters; PG203 near-end PMA loopback) and appear in peer-reviewed DAQ/network papers (HTSP self-loopback at 100G, P4TG feeding generated traffic back into its own ports at up to 1 Tb/s). The consistent claim boundary in accepted papers: single-board evaluation credibly supports engine throughput/latency, area/frequency, line-rate-sufficiency arguments (clock x width arithmetic stated explicitly), gate/scheduler behavior under emulated bandwidth, and trace-driven compression ratios — but NOT end-to-end application metrics (TTFT, training time) or congestion-control interactions, which accepted papers either omit or explicitly delegate to labeled simulation/analytical projection. The honest phrasing pattern is "meets timing at N Gbps" / "sufficient for line rate" / "emulated via payload shrinking" rather than "achieves N Gbps end-to-end". This maps cleanly onto an ISCAS 5-page paper: measured engine+transform+gate numbers on the VCU118 with an on-chip shaper sweep, plus a clearly-labeled analytical TTFT projection reusing the M3 frontier.
reports.details:
## Direct answer to the key question

| Claim | Single-board loopback eval can support? | Precedent |
|---|---|---|
| Compression/transform engine throughput, latency | YES (measured) | FCCM 2011/2015/2018 engines, AVED xbtest, NetZIP FPGA leg |
| Area, frequency, resource scaling | YES (post-PnR) | Tonic (NSDI'20), PIEO (SIGCOMM'19), 400G parser (ANCS'11) |
| Line-rate sufficiency ("meets timing at 100 Gbps") | YES (arithmetic bridge, stated explicitly) | Tonic abstract; PIEO Sec. 6.2 |
| Adaptive-gate behavior vs. bottleneck bandwidth | YES (on-chip generators + programmable rate limiter sweep) | PIEO Sec. 6.3 (0.1-32 Gbps token-bucket sweep, SIGCOMM-accepted) |
| Compression ratio on real traffic | YES (trace replay from DDR) | Covington FCCM'09, OSNT, FlueNT10G |
| Link BER / physical-path integrity | YES (QSFP loopback modules) | DTS-100G (BER<1e-12/24h), AVED |
| End-to-end application TTFT / job completion | NO — must be labeled simulation/analytical projection | NetZIP (SimAI), nanoPU (FireSim), Tonic (simulation) |
| Congestion-control / multi-tenant fabric effects | NO — no CC signals exist in loopback | all above avoid claiming it |
| Real observed wire-bandwidth change | NO — only emulated (payload shrinking / shaper) | NetZIP payload-shrinking emulation |

## (a) QSFP port-to-port / self-loopback on one board

- **HTSP, 100 Gb/s DAQ protocol** (arXiv 2203.15671, Xilinx U200): firmware output was looped back to itself with a fiber cable on the QSFP28 module for the performance evaluation — a peer-reviewed 100G protocol evaluated with a single board self-loopback. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2203.15671
- **P4TG traffic generator** (IEEE Access 2023, doi 10048513; Tofino ASIC): generates up to 1 Tb/s across 10x100G ports and validates itself by feeding generated traffic back from output to input ports, measuring rates, loss, reordering, IATs and RTTs *in the data plane* — same-device loopback as the entire evaluation of a hardware artifact. https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10048513/ , https://github.com/uni-tue-kn/P4TG
- **DTS-100G** (arXiv 2301.10706): QSFP28 characterized with 0.0 dB electrical loopback modules; 24-hour BER < 1e-12. Precedent for physical-path integrity claims from loopback modules alone. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.10706
- **RIFL link-layer protocol** (JOCN 2022; arXiv 2309.08696, Shen/Zheng/Chow, Toronto): 110 ns point-to-point latency at 112 Gbps over 10 m AOC, entirely in-lab FPGA-to-FPGA cabling with on-chip instrumentation, no host network stack. (Caveat: I could not fetch the full text to confirm single-board vs. two-board; the abstract confirms cable-connected FPGA evaluation with no switch/testbed.) https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.08696
- **Vendor methodology (AVED xbtest GT-MAC test, AMD)**: an embedded on-FPGA packet generator drives a card fitted with simple electrical or optical loopback cables; correctness and throughput come from per-lane 48-bit hardware packet/byte counters (RX_TOTAL_GOOD_PACKETS, TX_TOTAL_PACKETS, error registers). This is AMD's own production board-validation flow — exactly the (a)+(c)+(f) combination. https://xilinx.github.io/AVED/amd_v80_gen5x8_24.1_20241002/xbtest/user-guide/source/docs/test-cases/gt-mac-test-case-description.html

## (b) Internal MAC/PCS near-end loopback (cable-free)

- **Xilinx PG203 (UltraScale+ Integrated 100G Ethernet / CMAC)** documents near-end PMA loopback: the transmit path is routed to the receive path inside the package, before the transceiver pins — validated methodology for exercising the full 100G MAC datapath with no cable at all. Referenced/used by: MEEP project shell bring-up (https://meep-project.eu/media/news/meep-shell-part-1-ethernet-ip), the 100GBE-PYNQ project (https://github.com/JennySmith888/100GBE-PYNQ), and a Naval Postgraduate School RFSoC 100 GbE loopback study (https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/trecms/pdf/AD1156777.pdf). Use for: exercising the CMAC-attached datapath at full rate during development; not sufficient alone for physical-layer claims (use (a) for those).

## (c) On-chip traffic generators / trace replay from DDR

- **Covington et al., "A Packet Generator on the NetFPGA Platform" (FCCM 2009)**: a standard PCAP file is transferred to on-card SRAM/DRAM and replayed at line rate on 4x1G with user-specified precise data rate, inter-packet delay and iteration count; hardware timestamping inserted before the MAC FIFOs. The canonical peer-reviewed precedent for replaying captured traces from card memory. http://www.altusfidelitas.org/publications/NetFPGA_Packet_Generator_Stanford_FCCM_2009.pdf
- **OSNT (IEEE Network 2014, NetFPGA-10G)**: open-source tester; 4x10G generation across all packet sizes; 6.25 ns timestamp resolution, GPS-disciplined; generator and high-precision capture co-exist on a single card. https://osnt.org/files/osnt2014_fullpaper.pdf
- **FlueNT10G (FPL 2018)**: replays pre-recorded or synthetic traces with 6.4 ns temporal resolution (156.25 MHz MAC clock), captures and records per-packet round-trip latencies; streams trace data host->FPGA during the run so tests are not bounded by on-board memory. https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8533489/ , https://github.com/aoeldemann/fluent10g
- **PIEO (SIGCOMM 2019)**, inside the paper's own evaluation, Section 6.3: "We implement packet generators, one per flow, on the FPGA to simulate the flows." (link speed 40 Gbps, MTU granularity, 100 flows in a two-level hierarchy). SIGCOMM accepted a hardware scheduler paper whose *entire* traffic source is on-chip. https://engineering.purdue.edu/~vshriva/papers/pieo_2019.pdf
- **PANIC (OSDI 2020)**: 100 Gbps FPGA prototype (VU3P); the released artifact includes an on-FPGA packet generator and capture agent used to drive and measure the datapath (the paper also used a DPDK sender for some experiments). https://www.usenix.org/system/files/osdi20-lin.pdf , https://github.com/utnslab/PANIC

## (d) PCIe host-driven streaming benchmarks (compression-engine standard)

- **"High-Throughput, Lossless Data Compression on FPGAs" (FCCM 2011, IBM)**: sustained measured 2.66 GB/s on a PCIe FPGA board carrying two compression + two decompression engines (1 GB/s peak per engine) — throughput measured by streaming from the host over PCIe. https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/5771261/
- **Fowers et al. (FCCM 2015)**, scalable DEFLATE on Stratix V — the reference architecture for hardware deflate; evaluation is engine-level (corpus data in, compressed stream out), no network. https://people.ece.uw.edu/hauck/publications/Xpress8.pdf
- **UCLA CPU-FPGA deflate (FCCM 2018)**: 12.8 GB/s measured Deflate on a tightly-coupled CPU-FPGA platform, 16 bytes/cycle/way at 200 MHz — again host-driven streaming, engine-level claims only. https://vast.cs.ucla.edu/sites/default/files/publications/fccm2018-compression-camera_ready.pdf
- **"Gzip on a chip" (IWOCL 2014, Altera)**: ~3 GB/s OpenCL deflate, host-driven. https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2664666.2664670
- Norm established: for a compression engine, *nobody* requires a network testbed; corpus/trace data streamed over PCIe (or from DDR) with wall-clock or cycle-counter measurement is the accepted methodology at FCCM/FPL/DAC.

## (e) Programmable rate limiters / emulated bottleneck bandwidth

- **PIEO (SIGCOMM 2019) Sections 6.2-6.3 — the strongest precedent for the adaptive-gate claim**: token-bucket rate limiting programmed atop the FPGA prototype; rate limits assigned per node and swept across 0.1, 0.5, 2, 8, 16, 32 Gbps (Fig. 11 shows achieved rate tracking the configured limit across the sweep; Fig. 12 shows fair-queueing across 10 flows at each limit). Combined with the on-chip per-flow generators, this is a complete "behavior as a function of emulated link bandwidth" evaluation on one board, accepted at SIGCOMM. Also note the accepted arithmetic-bridge phrasing in 6.2: a primitive op every 50 ns at 80 MHz non-pipelined is *sufficient* to schedule MTU-sized packets at 100 Gbps line rate — a line-rate claim derived from clock math, not from wire measurement, stated transparently.
- **NetZIP (MICRO 2025, ACM doi 10.1145/3725843.3756079)**: FPGA-NIC prototype connected to commodity servers is used for *functional verification* and latency; the prototype has no RDMA stack and emulates compression benefit by payload shrinking; the 35% end-to-end training-time headline comes from SimAI simulation, and ASIC latency numbers are projections (verified against the full text earlier in this project, 2026-07-09; abstract at https://research.ibm.com/publications/netzip-algorithmhardware-co-design-of-in-network-lossless-compression-for-distributed-large-model-training). MICRO accepted this split explicitly.
- **Corundum (FCCM 2020)**: on-card TDMA scheduler creating 100 us timeslots demonstrates fine-grained hardware bandwidth shaping; note Corundum did use a minimal 2-node link (ConnectX-5 peer, 8x iperf3, 94.0 Gbps with TDMA off) for the NIC-datapath claim — the counter-example showing which claim (host-to-wire NIC throughput) does demand a peer. https://www.fccm.org/past/2020/proceedings/2020/pdfs/FCCM2020-65FOvhMqzyMYm99lfeVKyl/580300a038/580300a038.pdf

## (f) FPGA-internal instrumentation

- Hardware timestamp counters at MAC ingress/egress: Covington (pre-MAC-FIFO timestamping), OSNT (6.25 ns resolution, GPS/clock-drift coordination), FlueNT10G (6.4 ns, per-packet RTT), Corundum (native IEEE 1588 PTP timestamping in the datapath).
- In-datapath rate/latency measurement with no host in the loop: P4TG measures rates, IATs, RTTs directly in the data plane; AVED xbtest reads per-lane 48-bit MAC counters (good packets, bytes, error registers) via check_status.
- Cycle-accurate full-system alternative: nanoPU (OSDI 2021) ran the entire evaluation as FireSim cycle-exact simulation on AWS FPGAs (FPGA clock 90 MHz, simulated target 3.2 GHz), with a C++ Poisson load generator, and claimed 69 ns wire-to-wire RPC latency — accepted because the simulation methodology and clocks were stated precisely. https://www.usenix.org/system/files/osdi21-ibanez.pdf
- ILA norm: ILA/ChipScope is used for debug; published numbers come from free-running counters/CSRs read over AXI-Lite (AVED pattern). No accepted paper I found bases headline numbers on ILA captures.

## How accepted papers phrased the boundary honestly

1. **Tonic (NSDI 2020)**: abstract claims the prototype "meets timing" for 100 Gbps of back-to-back 128-byte packets on a Kintex UltraScale+ target — a synthesis/timing claim, deliberately not "we forwarded 100 Gbps of traffic"; protocol dynamics were evaluated in cycle-accurate simulation. https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi20/presentation/arashloo
2. **PIEO (SIGCOMM 2019)**: names its traffic as on-FPGA generators simulating flows; line-rate sufficiency presented as explicit clock arithmetic; scalability from post-synthesis ALM/SRAM/clock-rate curves (Figs. 8-10).
3. **NetZIP (MICRO 2025)**: hardware section = functional verification + engine latency on the FPGA-NIC; performance headline = simulation, clearly attributed to SimAI; ASIC = projection. The FPGA never carries a real RDMA/transport stack and the paper does not claim it does.
4. **nanoPU (OSDI 2021)**: every latency number is labeled as coming from cycle-accurate FireSim simulation with stated FPGA/target clock rates.
5. **P4TG / OSNT / FlueNT10G**: tester papers validate *themselves* by loopback and counter cross-checks — establishing loopback + hardware counters as a first-class measurement methodology in peer review.

## ISCAS norms and what this means for the WR-ZipGuard paper

ISCAS is a circuits venue: 5-page papers standardly present architecture + post-place-and-route area/frequency + throughput measured on-board or in RTL simulation, with no network testbed whatsoever (e.g., ISCAS-lineage FPGA IP-packet-compression network processor: 66 MHz, 32-bit datapath, 2 Gb/s effective line rate, implementation-results-only evaluation; ANCS 2011's 400 Gb/s programmable parser on a single FPGA was likewise implementation-results-only). A VCU118 single-board evaluation is *above* the ISCAS evidentiary bar, not below it.

Concrete, precedent-backed evaluation plan for the VCU118 (each element has a named precedent):
1. **Engine + forward-transform throughput/latency/area** on XCVU9P: corpus = captured real KV tensors (gpt2/Qwen2.5-7B/Llama-3.1-8B) streamed from host DDR/PCIe (FCCM 2011/2018 precedent) and from on-board DRAM replay (Covington/OSNT precedent).
2. **Line-rate sufficiency** stated as clock x datapath-width arithmetic against 100GbE CMAC beat rate (Tonic/PIEO phrasing).
3. **Adaptive-gate behavior**: on-chip token-bucket/credit shaper emulating bottleneck bandwidths swept e.g. 5-100 Gbps, on-chip generators replaying KV-transfer traces, gate decision quality + added latency measured by hardware timestamp counters (PIEO precedent — this exact experiment shape was accepted at SIGCOMM with zero external traffic).
4. **Physical-path validation**: QSFP28 cage-to-cage DAC/fiber loopback (HTSP/AVED precedent) and cable-free near-end PMA loopback (PG203) to run the full CMAC-attached pipeline; report per-lane MAC counters.
5. **End-to-end TTFT**: do NOT claim from the board. Present as a clearly-labeled analytical projection using the measured alpha, engine throughput, and the existing M3 profitability frontier (NetZIP's FPGA/SimAI split is the direct MICRO-2025 precedent; nanoPU/Tonic reinforce that labeled simulation/analysis is acceptable).
6. **Explicit limitations sentence** (pattern from the above): loopback evaluation demonstrates engine and gate behavior under emulated bandwidth; it does not demonstrate end-to-end application latency or interaction with transport congestion control, which are evaluated analytically/in simulation.

## Caveats / unverified items
- RIFL: single-board vs. two-board setup unconfirmed (PDF fetches timed out); abstract confirms cabled point-to-point FPGA evaluation, 110 ns @ 112 Gbps over 10 m AOC.
- Tonic's NS-3/cycle-accurate-simulator integration detail is from the abstract and search summaries; the USENIX PDF itself returned 403 — phrasing above sticks to what the abstract states ("meets timing", FPGA prototype, simulation-based protocol evaluation).
- Fowers FCCM 2015 exact headline numbers not re-verified (UW PDF cert failure); cited for methodology shape only.
- NetZIP full-text details (no RDMA stack, payload-shrinking emulation, 35% SimAI-only) come from this project's own 2026-07-09 full-text verification pass recorded in the repo (LITERATURE_REVIEW.md Section 1c / research_contract.md), consistent with the public abstract.

reports.summary: The broad claim "adaptive/selective compression decision-making in hardware is novel" is REFUTED many times over: shipping silicon already gates compression on estimated compressibility (Intel IAA's Early Abort circuitry checks after 512-4096 input bytes against a k/8 threshold and aborts; SandForce/LSI SSD controllers patented and shipped entropy-based detection of uncompressible data to bypass the compressor; WD/HGST patented a hash-bin + hit-counter hardware entropy detector that decides compress-vs-bypass in nanoseconds at ~10 mW), and even the NETWORK TX PATH variant is precedented in patents and deployed hardware (IBM US5555377, 1993: compress only when a token-ring adapter's hardware activity monitor sees >80% network utilization AND the block is >=4KB; 3Com US6763031, 1999: NIC-side demux/compressor/mux that compresses both versions and selects the smaller; ITU V.42bis modems since 1990 continuously monitor compressibility and auto-switch to transparent mode; RFC 3173 IPComp mandates per-packet non-expansion bypass with adaptive backoff, implemented in Hifn/Cisco compression hardware). However, NO prior art was found that implements the specific conjunction WR-ZipGuard proposes: a PRE-compression streaming compressibility estimator combined with a measured wire-time PROFITABILITY model (link bandwidth vs. compress/decompress engine throughput vs. achieved ratio, per-transfer arithmetic) as a synthesized circuit on a NIC/RDMA TX path emitting a lossless stream decodable by commodity NIC hardware. The closest modern academic work either always-compresses (SqueezeNIC NAIC'24, lossy), gates on a semantic FLAG not on data (NetZIP MICRO'25, 1-bit NCCL-header flag), or does the profitability math in software (AdOC HPDC'02; NEC patent US9807189's explicit "compress iff P·R_i·C_i >= N bandwidth" criterion). The recommendation for the ISCAS paper: do NOT claim "first hardware compression gate" or even "first on a network path"; claim the narrow conjunction (per-message, estimator-BEFORE-compression, bandwidth-parameterized wire-time gate, lossless commodity-decodable output), cite this lineage explicitly, and exploit it — the IAA-style early-abort and the WD-style entropy detector are implementable on the VCU118 as head-to-head baseline gate circuits, which turns the prior art into the paper's evaluation section.

# Prior Art Survey: Adaptive/Selective Compression Decision-Making in Hardware

## Verdict up front

| Claim | Status |
|---|---|
| "A hardware circuit that decides whether to compress is novel" | **REFUTED** (IAA, SandForce, WD patents, modems, routers) |
| "A data-dependent compression bypass on a network TX path in hardware is novel" | **REFUTED** (V.42bis 1990, IBM US5555377 1993, 3Com US6763031 1999, IPComp/Hifn) |
| "A compressibility ESTIMATOR circuit (not compress-then-compare) gating compression is novel" | **REFUTED** for storage (WD US9710166/US9946464, SandForce US8725933); **not found** for NIC path |
| "A per-message gate parameterized by MEASURED WIRE-TIME profitability (link BW x engine throughput x alpha) as a circuit on a NIC TX path, lossless + commodity-decodable" | **NOT FOUND — appears unclaimed as a conjunction** |

---

## (a) Storage / memory / datacenter compression silicon

### SandForce / LSI DuraWrite (shipped SSD controllers, ~2009-2014)
- DuraWrite is inline LZ77-class compression in the SSD controller; incompressible input is detected and passed through. LSI patent **US 8,725,933 "Method to detect uncompressible data in mass storage device"** (found via USPTO) covers detecting uncompressible data so "blind compression can be bypassed," saving bandwidth and power — the search summary states: "By identifying incompressible data, blind compression can be bypassed... with incompressible input data bypassing the compression module to write circuitry," and notes "high correlation between data entropy and data incompressibility."
- Well-documented behaviorally: incompressible (random/encrypted/media) data is the SF-1200/2200 worst case (Tom's Hardware, AnandTech-era reviews).
- **Mechanism class:** data-dependent hardware bypass in a storage controller write path.

### Western Digital / HGST hardware entropy detector — the closest ESTIMATOR circuit found
- **US 9,710,166 B2** (and sibling **US 9,946,464**) "Systems and methods for predicting compressibility of data," assignee Western Digital (orig. HGST): a **hardware entropy detector** in the flash controller. Exact mechanism (from patent text):
  - extracts 2-byte intervals from the block; a hash maps "only 11 of the 16 bits of the two byte interval" into **~2048 bins** with **11-bit hit counters**;
  - a duplicate mapping to an occupied bin increments the hit count;
  - ratio of hits to total intervals compared to a **~45-50% threshold**: "If the ratio is greater than the preselected threshold, the data block can be compressed. If not, the data block can be left un-compressed."
  - claimed performance: decision in "nanoseconds" vs milliseconds in software, **~10 mW** vs 1-1.5 W for actually compressing.
- **This is a per-block, pre-compression, streaming compressibility-estimator gate as a circuit** — everything WR-ZipGuard's gate does EXCEPT the wire-time/bandwidth term and the network location. Must be cited; also an ideal baseline to re-implement on the VCU118.

### Intel IAA (In-Memory Analytics Accelerator, Sapphire Rapids+) — shipping datacenter silicon with a compressibility gate
- IAA Architecture Specification (intel cdrdv2 350295) documents **"Early Abort"** for compression, controlled by Compression 2 Flags: the **Early Abort Size field** makes the compressor check "as soon as 512, 1024, 2048, or 4096 input bytes have been processed."
- Intel patent **US 12,405,893 B2 "Technology for early abort of compression acceleration"** gives the circuit mechanism: "the estimate of the compressed size is the number of literals plus twice the number of references" (Deflate tokens, headers disregarded); threshold is a 3-bit field encoding required savings of "at least 12.5%, ... 87.5%" (k/8); on failure "early-abort circuitry 24 aborts compression operations without processing the rest of the source data" and returns an abort code (caller then stores/sends raw — the zswap use case).
- **Mechanism class:** compress-then-abort (the estimator IS the running compressor), threshold in eighths, sample window 512-4096 B. Not pre-compression estimation, not network-located, no bandwidth term. Closest MODERN silicon analog. Also note patent **US 9,531,403 "Adaptive compression supporting output size thresholds"** (same family space).

### IBM MXT (main-memory compression, Pinnacle chipset, IBM JRD 45(2), 2001)
- Hardware LZ-derivative (X-Match/parallel block-referential) compressing 1KB lines into variable numbers of 256B sectors; lines that do not compress below a threshold are stored unmodified (the 1:1 end of its "1:1-64:1" range). Sector-based allocator handles the variable size. Decision is a size-outcome check in the memory controller, not an estimator. (IBM JRD "IBM Memory Expansion Technology (MXT)," Tremaine et al.)

### Cache/memory-compression academia — cost-benefit gating in hardware proposals
- **Alameldeen & Wood, "Adaptive Cache Compression for High-Performance Processors," ISCA 2004**: a global saturating counter predictor updated per-access with the estimated benefit (misses avoided by compression) vs cost (decompression latency) — literally an online **profitability estimator in hardware**, deciding whether to store L2 lines compressed. Domain = cache latency, not wire time.
- **BPC (Kim, Sullivan, Choukse, Erez, "Bit-Plane Compression," ISCA 2016)**: per-block transformed compression for GPU memory BW with uncompressed fallback for non-matching words ("Code words that cannot match any of the patterns... are stored uncompressed") — fallback, not a gate.
- **CRAM (arXiv 1807.07685)**: hardware memory compression for bandwidth with a line-compressibility predictor claimed at **98% accuracy** deciding fetch behavior.
- **ICCD 2016 "Enabling Technologies for Memory Compression: Metadata, Mapping, and Prediction"** (Utah): per-line compressibility prediction to size memory fetches.
- Patents: **US 12,066,935 "Cache line compression prediction and adaptive compression"**; **US 7,412,564 "Adaptive cache compression system"** (predictor controls compression "based on predicted effect of compression on program execution speed").
- Note the request mentioned CAMEO — CAMEO (MICRO 2014) is stacked-DRAM cache management, not compression gating; the relevant selective-compression lineage is Alameldeen/Wood -> C-Pack-era selective caches ("only lines with ratio < 0.5 are compressed") -> CRAM.

### Datacenter compression ASICs
- **Microsoft Project Zipline / Corsica ASIC** (Azure+Broadcom, 100 Gbps compression+crypto; RTL open-sourced via OCP): public materials document ratio/throughput/latency claims ("more than 20 percent higher compression ratios versus Zlib-L4 64KB", multiple pipelines to 100Gbps) but **no documented data-driven per-block compression bypass** in the public blog/RTL descriptions. (One secondary summary suggested it "avoids hash-table lookups when data appears incompressible" as a cycle-saving optimization — I could not verify this in a primary source; treat as unverified.) DEFLATE stored-block fallback (emit raw blocks) is format-level table stakes in all these engines, distinct from not spending compression work.
- **IBM z15 zEDC / Nest Accelerator Unit (NXU)**: on-chip DEFLATE invoked synchronously by the DFLTCC instruction; **software decides** (default: accelerate compression only at level 1; `DFLTCC_LEVEL_MASK` env var extends to other levels; millicode chunks data at 256KB). No data-driven hardware gate documented. (IBM docs + ISCA 2020 "Data compression accelerator on IBM POWER9 and z15 processors".)
- **Intel QAT**: job-based; incompressible-data handling is software policy (e.g., QATzip fallback). No documented on-chip pre-compression gate — the gate innovation landed in IAA instead (above).
- **ScaleFlux CSD / Pliops XDP**: inline transparent compression in the drive/controller; public FAQs acknowledge "Encrypted data and 100% incompressible data will reduce performance & endurance" — i.e., behavior consistent with compress-always or size-outcome fallback; **no documented entropy-estimator gate**.
- **Tape drives (LTO SLDC / IBM IDRC lineage)**: hardware compressors since the 1980s-90s with per-record protection against expansion (SLDC scheme switching / literal pass-through encoding: "When data can't be compressed SLDC represents all bytes as themselves"); drives guarantee incompressible data costs ~0% (LTO) capacity overhead — an in-silicon anti-expansion mechanism decades old.

## (b) NICs / DPUs / network path

### Deployed / standardized per-packet gating on the wire — the strongest location-precedent
- **ITU-T V.42bis modems (1990)**: the standard REQUIRES continuous compressibility monitoring in the modem: the algorithm "constantly monitors the compressibility of the data" and automatically switches between **compressed mode and transparent mode** (escape-code signaled), both directions. Implemented in modem chipsets/firmware for 35 years. Data-driven, online, link-path hardware — but per-stream/continuous, ratio-only criterion (link rate fixed, so ratio == wire-time profit), no per-message granularity. See also patent **US 7,263,233 "Apparatus and method for data compressibility test."**
- **RFC 3173 IPComp (2001)**, implemented in Hifn security/compression processors and Cisco Compression Service Adapters (LZS/MPPC in hardware): exact normative text: "If the total size of a compressed payload and the IPComp header... is not smaller than the size of the original payload, the IP datagram MUST be sent in the original non-compressed form." Plus a size threshold ("IP datagrams of size smaller than the threshold are sent in the original form without attempting compression") and an **adaptive backoff**: "if the compression of i consecutive IP datagrams of an IPCA fails, the next several IP datagrams, say k, are sent without attempting compression. If then the next j datagrams also fail to compress, a larger number... k+n, are sent without attempting compression." RFC 1967 (LZS-DCP) similarly documents the "anti-expansion mechanism" (max LZS expansion 12.5%). **Per-packet, hardware-executed, TX-path — but compress-then-compare + counter backoff, no estimator, no bandwidth term.**
- **IBM patent US 5,555,377 (filed 1993)** — "System for selectively compressing data transferred in network...": compression is enabled when a token-ring **communications adapter's hardware "network activity monitor circuit"** (counting busy tokens per interval) reports utilization above a first threshold (~80%, hysteresis to ~70%) AND the block exceeds a 4KB minimum. Decision split between adapter hardware monitor + adapter microcode + host protocol stack. **This is a wire-state-dependent selective-compression gate on a network adapter, 33 years ago.** It lacks any data-compressibility estimation and any engine-throughput arithmetic, but it kills any claim that "compress-only-when-the-wire-makes-it-profitable, decided at the adapter" is new in kind.
- **3Com patent US 6,763,031 B1 (filed 1999)** — "Network device incorporating selective compression of stored data packets": hardware TX datapath with a **demultiplexer that routes the payload (after the first 38 header bytes) through a compressor**, and two strategies: (Fig.2) size threshold — packets <=256B bypass; (Fig.3) **compress AND store both versions in parallel FIFOs, comparator selects the shorter** ("criterion is the size of said versions, smaller thereof being selected"). **A data-dependent hardware compress-or-bypass mux on a network device — the single closest structural precedent to a NIC TX-path gate circuit.**
- Generic patents also exist: US 8,001,278 (network adapter payload compression logic "hardware, software, or combination"), US 8,355,399 (traffic-shaper selective compression), US 20160037509.

### Modern SmartNICs / DPUs — NO data-driven compression gating found
- **Microsoft AccelNet (NSDI 2018)**: canonical per-flow offload gating — first packet of a flow traverses the software VFP slow path, policy is compiled into the FPGA **GFT** flow cache, subsequent packets hit hardware. **Control-plane, per-flow, not data-dependent, and not compression.**
- **NVIDIA BlueField-3** (from this project's own M2 measurements): DOCA compress/decompress is **job-queue based; host/DPU software decides per job**; no data-driven auto-gate (and BF3 exposes decompress-only in this deployment).
- **AMD Pensando, Fungible F1, Marvell OCTEON** (ZIP coprocessor blocks since OCTEON II): compression/decompression engines are documented as offload engines fed by software work queues (storage/analytics use). **No public documentation of per-packet or per-message data-dependent compression gating** in any of these. (Vendor product briefs + DPU surveys; absence-of-evidence claim.)
- **NetZIP (MICRO 2025, IBM Research + academia; ACM DOI 10.1145/3725843.3756079)** — closest contemporary academic system: bump-in-the-wire FPGA-NIC lossless compression for gradients/activations (bit/value-level transforms + lightweight standard codec; claims 35% training-time reduction, SimAI-scale). Its gate is **flag-driven, not data-driven**: a modified NCCL header carries a 1-bit compress flag + 15-bit layer ID; the NIC obeys the flag. Per this project's 2026-07-09 full-text verification: sits upstream of the NIC protocol engine, per-4KB-packet self-contained, no RDMA/verbs semantics, FPGA prototype without an RDMA stack, BF-2 ARM detour 11x worse. **It does not estimate compressibility and has no profitability model.**
- **SqueezeNIC (SIGCOMM NAIC workshop 2024)**: FPGA NIC in-line **lossy** (quantization) gradient compression at line rate, 1.21x training speedup — **always compresses; no selective/bypass logic** found in the paper.
- **ZipCCL (arXiv 2604.27844, 2026)**: GPU-side lossless collective compression with "adaptive communication strategies that dynamically switch collective operations" — adaptivity is at the collective-algorithm level, in software, on GPU; not a NIC circuit.

### Software wire-time profitability models (concept precedents, not circuits)
- **AdOC (Jeannot et al., HPDC 2002 / IPDPS 2005)**: adaptive online compression library that "automatically adapts the compression effort to currently available network and processor resources" — the canonical compress-vs-send-raw wire-time tradeoff, in software.
- **NEC patent US 9,807,189 B2**: explicit profitability criterion — select algorithm i as CPU-constrained iff "P·R_i·C_i >= N" (parallelism x compression speed x ratio vs network bandwidth). **This is WR-ZipGuard's gate equation, patented — in software.** Must be cited and differentiated (per-transfer circuit vs host library; measured decompressor constraint; verbs semantics).
- **Harnik et al., "To Zip or Not to Zip" (FAST 2013, IBM)**: compressibility-estimation heuristics (sampling + byte-statistics) "to estimate compression ratios and use it as the deciding factor" for real-time storage compression; shipped in IBM storage (RtC/Comprestimator lineage). Software, storage-side — but the estimator design directly informs a hardware estimator.

## (c) Academic entropy/compressibility estimation as a circuit (2015-2026)
- **P4/Tofino entropy estimation at line rate**: "Tracking Normalized Network Traffic Entropy to Detect DDoS Attacks in P4" (arXiv 2104.05117; P4NEntropy/P4DDoS) — normalized Shannon entropy computed in the match-action pipeline; sketch/tabular-interpolation variants (EuroP4'22, ACM 3565475.3569082) deployed on **Tofino2 estimating traffic entropy at 400 Gbps**. Entropy of HEADER-FIELD distributions for security, not payload compressibility, and in a switch not a NIC TX offload — but proves streaming entropy estimation is line-rate feasible in network silicon.
- **WD US9710166/US9946464** (detailed above) is also the key academic-adjacent circuit blueprint: hash-bin histogram + hit-counter ratio, 2048 bins, 11-bit counters.
- FPGA compression accelerators 2015-2026 (LpaqHP ICPP'24, Snappy-on-FPGA Electronics 2025, Golomb-Rice camera pipelines, etc.) accelerate the CODEC, not the decision; none surveyed implements a standalone compressibility-prediction prefilter for a network path.
- **No published FPGA/ASIC paper was found implementing "payload compressibility estimation -> compress/bypass gate" on a NIC TX path.** The building blocks all exist separately (Tofino entropy at 400G; WD estimator in an SSD controller; IAA early-abort in a memory accelerator).

---

## The 3 closest pieces of prior art (ranked by threat to the novelty claim)

**1. Intel IAA Early Abort (shipping silicon + spec + patent US 12,405,893).** Hardware gate inside a datacenter accelerator: runs Deflate on the first 512/1024/2048/4096 bytes, estimates output as (#literals + 2x#references), compares against a configurable k/8 savings threshold, and aborts the job so the caller handles the data raw. *Gap vs WR-ZipGuard:* the estimator is the compressor itself (pays compression cost on the sample), it is memory/storage-side (zswap/RocksDB), and the threshold is a pure ratio — no link-bandwidth/wire-time term, no NIC/TX placement, no per-transfer transport semantics.

**2. WD/HGST hardware entropy detector, US 9,710,166 / US 9,946,464 (+ shipped SandForce US 8,725,933).** A true pre-compression streaming estimator circuit: 2-byte-interval hashing into 2048 bins, 11-bit hit counters, hit-ratio vs ~45-50% threshold decides compress-vs-bypass in nanoseconds at ~10 mW, in an SSD controller write path. *Gap:* storage write path, ratio-threshold only (no bandwidth/engine-throughput arithmetic), block- not message-granular, no network semantics. This is simultaneously the best baseline to reimplement on the VCU118.

**3. Network-TX-path selective compression hardware: 3Com US 6,763,031 (1999) + IBM US 5,555,377 (1993) + IPComp-in-Hifn/Cisco silicon.** Together these cover: a hardware demux/compressor/comparator/mux on a network device selecting the smaller of compressed/uncompressed versions per packet (3Com); a network-adapter gate keyed on MEASURED WIRE STATE (token-ring utilization >80% + >=4KB size) (IBM); and standardized per-packet non-expansion bypass with adaptive backoff executed by deployed compression NIC hardware (RFC 3173/RFC 1967, Hifn LZS, Cisco CSA). *Gap:* none estimates compressibility before compressing (3Com compresses both and compares; IBM ignores data content entirely; IPComp compresses then checks), none combines data-dependent AND wire-state-dependent terms into one profitability computation, all predate RDMA/verbs semantics and multi-hundred-Gbps asymmetric engines.

*(Honorable mentions: NetZIP MICRO'25 — closest application domain, gate is flag- not data-driven; Alameldeen & Wood ISCA'04 — closest "online cost/benefit profitability estimator in hardware," wrong domain (cache latency); NEC US 9,807,189 — the exact profitability inequality, in software; V.42bis — oldest link-path hardware compressibility monitor.)*

## What survives for the ISCAS paper (recommended claim shape)

Claimable conjunction (no single prior work found with all of these): **(i)** per-message/per-transfer granularity on a NIC-style TX datapath, **(ii)** streaming compressibility ESTIMATION before/without running the full compressor (histogram/entropy prefilter a la WD, but message-granular and wire-facing), **(iii)** a profitability gate parameterized by MEASURED platform numbers — link bandwidth, FPGA compress throughput, commodity-decompressor (BF3 ~188 Gbps) constraint, transform cost T_xform/T_inv — i.e., wire-time arithmetic in the gate circuit, not just a ratio threshold, **(iv)** lossless, single standard deflate stream decodable by commodity NIC hardware. Framing guidance: cite the full lineage above and position the contribution as "the first message-granular wire-time-profitability gate circuit for lossless NIC-path compression," explicitly contrasting: IAA = compress-then-abort ratio gate (no wire model); WD/SandForce = entropy gate (storage, no wire model); IBM'93/3Com'99/IPComp = wire- or size-gates (no estimator, no engine-rate arithmetic); NetZIP = flag gate (no data dependence). Evaluation gift: implement (1) always-compress, (2) IAA-style early-abort, (3) WD-style entropy-threshold, (4) proposed profitability gate on the VCU118 and compare gate accuracy (vs oracle wire-time), latency, LUT/FF/BRAM area, and power — this converts the dense prior art from a threat into the paper's baseline suite, and none of it requires a second host/NIC since the gate decision quality can be scored against recorded KV-cache traces and the measured-parameter wire-time model.

reports.summary: Direct answer: (1) No one has published an FPGA-validated sender-side pipeline that emits a commodity-decodable standard-deflate stream for KV or tensor transfer — the pieces all exist separately (NetZIP puts LZ4/Snappy compression in an FPGA-NIC but for training gradients, with no RDMA stack in the prototype and simulation-only end-to-end numbers; ShadowServe consumes standard deflate on BlueField-3's hardware decompress engine but on the receive side of a lossy quantize-then-deflate prefix-cache pipeline; commercial FPGA deflate IPs like CAST ZipAccel-C prove 100+ Gbps encode feasibility but with no tensor transform, no gate, no KV context), so the transform + standard-deflate + gate sender combination is an open gap. (2) No data-driven compress-or-bypass gate exists in NIC hardware in the academic literature: the closest are TRACE/CXL-NDP's "raw bypass when not profitable" inside a simulated/RTL-synthesized CXL memory controller, UCCL-Zip's software >1 MB size threshold, NetZIP's flag-driven (not data-driven) header gate, and 2010s-era industry patents (Juniper US8750370, Intel US10728311) that a paper should cite to pre-empt novelty attacks while claiming the measured-frontier, per-WR-cost-accounting hardware gate. (3) The three nearest attack-surface papers are ShadowServe (arXiv 2509.16857; real BF3 testbed but single machine with a rate-limited ConnectX-7, lossy, receive-side), NetZIP (MICRO 2025; FPGA-NIC prototype without RDMA stack, headline 35% from SimAI simulation, training-only), and TRACE/CXL-NDP (IEEE TC 2026; DRAMSim3 + 7 nm RTL synthesis only, memory-tier not network). Every one of these evaluates with single-node testbeds, emulated bandwidth, or pure simulation, so a single-VCU118 eval (measured pipeline throughput/latency/resources + measured-parameter frontier model) is squarely within community norms and can be positioned as *more* hardware-validated than NetZIP's headline or TRACE's synthesis. Bonus corroboration found: ShadowServe's profitable region is explicitly "<= 20 Gbps," independently confirming the project's M3 narrow-frontier finding, and SplitZip's baseline table shows nvCOMP LZ4 achieves ratio 1.019 (~nothing) on raw BF16 KV, confirming transform-first necessity. Ecosystem status July 2026: what ships is still lossy (CacheGen in LMCache, KVTC "soon" in Dynamo KVBM per GTC 2026); LMCache's new MP-mode SERDE interface now lets lossless lz4/zstd be plugged in software, but no hardware, no gating, no deflate-on-NIC.
