# Survey: NIC/FPGA/network offloads for LLM serving and KV-cache movement (2025–2026)

## 1. Paper-by-paper findings (primary-source verified)

### 1.1 NetZIP — MICRO 2025 (in-network training-gradient compression)
- **Full title/venue**: "NetZIP: Algorithm/Hardware Co-design of In-network Lossless Compression for Distributed Large Model Training", MICRO '25 (Huang, ... Nam Sung Kim, UIUC + IBM). DOI 10.1145/3725843.3756079 (ACM DL returns 403 to anonymous fetch; abstract verified via IBM Research page). No arXiv preprint found.
- **What it does**: two parts — "NetZIP-algorithm transforms gradients and activations at the bit and value levels" so that "lightweight standard lossless compression" achieves more compression; "NetZIP-accelerator integrates NetZIP-algorithm with a lightweight lossless compression accelerator within a NIC in a bump-in-the-wire fashion."
- **Codec**: LZ4/Snappy ("LZ4 or Snappy is the best choice for implementing NetZIP-accelerator") — **not deflate, not commodity-decodable by an unmodified receiver**; both ends need the custom NIC.
- **Numbers (public)**: gradients/activations compressed "40–63 and 43–75 percentage points more" than heavy standard compression on Llama-3 70B / GPT-3 175B / Llama-3 405B; "NetZIP reduces the total training time by 35%".
- **Eval reality** (public record is thin; our own prior full-text verification, 2026-07-09, remains the sharpest source): FPGA-NIC prototype has **no RDMA stack** (payload-shrinking emulation); the **35% headline is simulation-only (SimAI)**; gate is **flag-driven** via a modified-NCCL header (1-bit flag + 15-bit layer ID), i.e., the sender's software decides, not the data; compression sits upstream of the NIC protocol engine so it never faces the verbs contract; BF-2 Arm-detour measured 11x worse (confirms inline-or-die).
- **Scope**: training gradients/activations only; no KV cache, no inference.

### 1.2 TRACE / CXL-NDP — IEEE Trans. on Computers (April 2026 issue), arXiv 2509.03377
- v2 retitled "Amplifying Effective CXL Memory Bandwidth for LLM Inference via Transparent Near-Data Processing" (CXL-NDP); IEEE CS page keeps "TRACE: Unlocking Effective CXL Bandwidth via Lossless Compression and Precision Scaling".
- **Mechanism**: channel-major, bit-plane-disaggregated KV layout inside the CXL device ("we organize KV vectors by aligning entries at the same position across all tokens in the group, thereby forming a matrix structure for each channel"), then commodity codecs.
- **Codec + gate**: "LZ4 is used for low latency, ZSTD for higher ratio, with **raw bypass when not profitable**" — this is the closest published compress-or-bypass gate, but it lives in a **CXL memory controller**, not a NIC, and is not driven by a measured network frontier.
- **Eval**: **no FPGA prototype, no silicon** — DRAMSim3 simulation ("precision-proportional fetch lowers DRAM access energy by up to 40.3%") + "RTL synthesis in a 7 nm process ... 2 TB/s throughput requires only about 5.7 mm²" + end-to-end serving model (43% throughput gain).
- **Ratio**: overall KV lossless ratios "1.81 on WikiText and 1.88 on BookSum" for BF16 (alpha ~0.53–0.55).
- **Network**: "No mention of NIC or network transfer" — exclusively CXL device-internal.

### 1.3 ShadowServe — arXiv 2509.16857 (SmartNIC-accelerated prefix caching)
- "First SmartNIC-accelerated, interference-free prefix caching system for LLM serving."
- **Hardware**: "NVIDIA BlueField-3 DPU" with "16-core Arm Cortex-A78AE processor and 32GB DDR5 memory", featuring "a lossless decompression accelerator for both Deflate and LZ4 algorithms" and P2P DMA to GPU. **This is published proof that BF3's hardware deflate decompress engine works on (quantized) KV data — directly legitimizing the commodity-deflate-decode premise.**
- **Codec**: CacheGen-style "vector-wise data binning for quantization" + "lossless compression using the Deflate algorithm"; "Deflate ... achieves a superior compression ratio on the quantized KV cache data compared to LZ4". Overall pipeline is **lossy** (quantization first). Decompression on SmartNIC only; compression happens off the critical path at cache-store time, **not sender-side, not FPGA, not per-transfer**.
- **Eval setup**: **single machine** — NVIDIA L40S GPU, 2x Xeon Gold 6526Y, "dual-port Mellanox ConnectX-7 400 Gbps NIC" **with rate limiting** to emulate low bandwidth; PCIe 4.0 x16.
- **Results**: "up to 2.2x lower loaded TPOT", "reduces TTFT by up to 1.38x in **low-bandwidth scenarios (<= 20 Gbps)**", "up to 1.35x higher throughput"; vs CacheGen-Async at 20 Gbps: 16% lower unloaded TTFT. **The <= 20 Gbps profitable region independently corroborates WR-ZipGuard's M3 frontier (B_crit ~6–21 Gbps).**

### 1.4 UCCL-Zip — arXiv 2604.17172 (April 2026)
- GPU ANS compression fused into P2P (Uzip-P2P split-send pipeline) and NCCL persistent kernels (Uzip-NCCL).
- **Ratios**: bf16 ~0.68 (elsewhere "stable ~64%"), fp32 0.85, fp16 ~0.83, float8_e5m2 ~0.70, float8_e4m3fn ~0.77.
- **Gate**: size threshold only — "Compression is enabled only for messages larger than 1 MB" (software, not data-driven).
- **Decodability**: **custom GPU ANS decoder required** (warp-level, localized frequency tables) — not commodity-decodable.
- **Eval**: real testbed — "two p5en.48xlarge instances" (8x H200 each) over "16x EFA (200 Gbps)"; also AMD MI355X/RoCEv2 and 8x L40S.
- **KV relevance**: yes — "KV cache transfer latency under prefill–decode disaggregation (P1D3) in vLLM", "up to 30.1% improvement"; RL weight sync +47.5%; vLLM E2E latency -10%.

### 1.5 SplitZip — arXiv 2605.01708v3 (23 Jun 2026, Notre Dame) — PDF verified page-by-page
- Fixed-length top-16 exponent codebook (4-bit codes, offline calibrated) + explicit escape stream (position, raw exponent); sign+mantissa stored raw. CR = 2/(3/2+3eps), asymptote 4/3.
- **Ratios (Table 1/2, exact)**: BF16 realized CR 1.31–1.33x across Qwen3-30B-A3B/32B/Next-80B, Llama-3.1-70B/3-8B, Phi-2 (alpha ~0.75–0.76); **E5M2 1.14x** (alpha ~0.877, "approximately 88% of the theoretical maximum compression for E5M2 (from the 6.19-bit raw byte entropy)"). SplitZip overall table ratio 1.324.
- **Throughput**: "613.3 GB/s encoding and 2181.8 GB/s decoding" on H200. Baselines in the same table: **nvCOMP LZ4 ratio 1.019, nvCOMP Cascaded 1.000, nvCOMP Bitcomp 1.056**, ZipNN 1.515, DFloat11 1.423, Falcon 1.428, ZipServ 1.236. (Generic byte-codecs on raw BF16 KV do ~nothing — a quantitative gift for the transform-first argument.)
- **Eval**: single server (H200 + dual Xeon Platinum 8468, ConnectX-7 IB adapters); SGLang on Mooncake transport, "RoCE 4x200G configuration with 700 Gb/s effective payload bandwidth"; E2E "up to 1.32x faster BF16 KV cache transfer, 1.30x faster TTFT, 1.23x higher request throughput."
- **Decodability**: custom GPU codec, not commodity-decodable. No hardware gate. Note: WR-ZipGuard's BF16 byte-transpose deflate alpha ~0.705 and e5m2 chan 0.704 both beat SplitZip's ratios while remaining BF3-decodable (positioning gift confirmed, now with v3 numbers).

### 1.6 KVFetcher — arXiv 2602.09725 ("Efficient Remote KV Cache Reuse with GPU-native Video Codec", Feb 2026)
- Uses GPU media ASICs (NVENC/NVDEC, AMD AMF, Intel QSV) for KV compress/decompress: "The encoding follows H.265 with lossless=1 to skip lossy steps" — **a sender-side ASIC compressor emitting a commodity(video)-decodable stream, but a video bitstream (not deflate), on GPU media engines (not the NIC path), for prefix-cache reuse (not PD transfer)**.
- Eval: A100 (5 NVDECs), H20 (7), L20 (3); LWM-7B/Yi-34B/Llama3-70B; **1–40 Gbps emulated networks**. Results: "1.52–3.51x TTFT reduction compared to SOTA methods"; vs CacheGen 77% TTFT reduction; CacheGen decompression contention costs "50% increase in prefilling time".
- Attacks ShadowServe on cost: "prohibitive deployment costs (>$3000 of each NVIDIA BlueField NIC)". Cites concurrent **llm.265** ("Video codecs are secretly tensor codecs", MICRO 2025) and beats it by "1.41x compression ratio" improvement. (Absolute ratio not extracted; fetch of full text repeatedly timed out — verify before citing numbers beyond these.)

### 1.7 CXL-SpecKV — FPGA 2026, arXiv 2512.11920
- "First CXL-based disaggregated memory architecture specifically designed for LLM KV-cache management" with **real hardware**: "4x Intel Agilex-7 FPGAs (933K ALMs, 64GB HBM per device, 1.6TB/s bandwidth) with CXL 2.0 controllers"; post-P&R fmax 812 MHz.
- Compression: **INT8 quantization + delta + RLE, 3.21x** with "+1.2% perplexity degradation" — i.e., **lossy overall** despite the lossless delta/RLE stage (attackable if cited against a bit-exact claim). CXL memory tier, **not NIC/network**. Headline: 3.2x throughput vs GPU-only, +8.2% per-token latency.

### 1.8 SmartNIC serving-stack offloads (no compression)
- **Blink** (arXiv 2604.07609): "CPU-free LLM inference by delegating the serving stack to GPU and SmartNIC" — SmartNIC does request handling + RDMA into GPU memory; persistent GPU kernel does batching/scheduling/KV management. P99 TTFT up to 8.47x better pre-saturation vs TensorRT-LLM/vLLM/SGLang. No compression component.
- **ICMSP** (CES 2026, industry): BlueField-4 DPUs manage KV movement off the GPU path — movement/tiering, not compression.
- **FpgaNIC** (ATC'22, RC4ML) remains the reference GPU-centric FPGA SmartNIC (100 Gb, GPUDirect P2P); no direct successor targeting LLM KV transfer compression found; follow-on platform work is **FpgaHub** (arXiv 2503.09318). Corundum remains the standard open-source 100G FPGA NIC substrate ("Academic labs use Corundum to explore new protocols (e.g., RDMA over Converged Ethernet)"); it provides queues/DMA/PTP but **no congestion-control algorithms**, consistent with the premise that no transport CC signal is available to a gate on open FPGA NICs.

### 1.9 Framework/ecosystem transfer-path status (July 2026)
- **LMCache**: CacheGen merged (lossy quant+entropy). New in 2026: MP-mode SERDE — "Anything lossless (lz4/zstd) or lossy (CacheGen-style) can be plugged in via the Serializer / Deserializer ABCs" (docs.lmcache.ai/mp/serde.html); 2026 Q2 roadmap (GitHub issue #2923) ships the modular interface. **Update nuance for our claim**: "what ships is lossy" still holds for defaults, but a software plug-point for lossless lz4/zstd now exists — phrase as "no hardware, no gating, no deflate-on-NIC; lossless remains a software plug-in slot, not a shipped codec."
- **NVIDIA Dynamo/KVBM + KVTC**: KVTC published at ICLR 2026 (transform coding, **lossy**, up to 20x, <1% accuracy loss); GTC 2026 (March) session + press: "an optimized implementation will soon be integrated into the KV Block Manager (KVBM)" — still "soon", not shipped as of July 2026. Watch item confirmed unchanged.
- **Mooncake/SGLang/vLLM**: 2026 news is transfer plumbing, not compression — SGLang RDMA P2P weight transfer via Mooncake TransferEngine (Apr 29, 2026, 7x faster Kimi-K2 weight sync); vLLM MoRIIO KV connector blog (Apr 7, 2026); vLLM per-layer RDMA writes of KV. No lossless KV codec merged into any of them.
- **BlueField-3 capability record**: DOCA Compress docs + HotI'23 "Compression Analysis for BlueField-2/-3" (NSF PAR 10538184) document the deflate C-engine; current BF3 DOCA exposes deflate/LZ4 **decompress**; compress-on-BF3 unsupported (matches our M2 hardware measurement; ShadowServe likewise only uses the decompress accelerator).

## 2. Answers to the key questions

### Q1 — FPGA-validated sender-side compression emitting a commodity-decodable standard-deflate stream for KV/tensor transfer?
**No.** Decomposition of the closest evidence:
| Piece | Who has it | What's missing vs our pipeline |
|---|---|---|
| FPGA-NIC inline lossless compression for ML traffic | NetZIP (MICRO'25) | LZ4/Snappy not deflate; training gradients not KV; prototype has no RDMA stack; E2E headline is SimAI simulation; symmetric custom NICs (receiver is not commodity) |
| Standard deflate consumed by commodity NIC hardware on KV data | ShadowServe (2509.16857) | Receive-side only; stream is quantized first (lossy); compression is software at store time; no gate |
| Sender-side ASIC compression, commodity-decodable stream | KVFetcher (2602.09725) / llm.265 (MICRO'25) | H.265 video bitstream, not deflate; GPU media engines, not NIC path; prefix reuse, not PD transfer |
| 100+ Gbps deflate encode on FPGA | CAST ZipAccel-C (claims >400 Gbps feasible), MetaZip (DAC'22, 15.6 GB/s), HLS deflate accelerators | Generic IP; no float/KV transform, no gate, no transfer integration, no LLM eval |
| Dtype-aware transform + commodity codec in hardware context | TRACE/CXL-NDP (IEEE TC'26) | CXL memory controller; DRAMSim3 + 7nm synthesis, no FPGA prototype; LZ4/ZSTD not a NIC-decodable deflate stream; no network |

The combination — **sender FPGA implementing (byte-transpose / channel-major) transform + RFC1951 deflate + gate, emitting one standard stream a stock BlueField-3 decompress engine can consume, bit-exact, for KV transfer** — is unpublished. That is the paper's gap statement, and ShadowServe conveniently proves the receiver half exists in deployed silicon.

### Q2 — Data-driven compress-or-bypass gate in NIC hardware?
**No published academic instance.** Prior art to cite defensively:
- **TRACE/CXL-NDP**: "raw bypass when not profitable" — nearest published gate; memory-controller context, simulation/synthesis only.
- **NetZIP**: gate exists but is **flag-driven** (modified-NCCL header bit set by software), not data-driven.
- **UCCL-Zip**: ">1 MB" size threshold (software); **ZipCCL** (2604.27844): "adaptive communication strategies that dynamically switch collective operations" (software, 64-GPU training cluster).
- **Patents** (must-cite to pre-empt novelty attack): Juniper US8750370 "Congestion-adaptive compression" (compress more when congested); Intel US10728311 "adaptive payload compression in a network fabric" (link-load-based); compressibility-prediction patents US20140244604A1 / US9946464; academic "Low-Overhead Compressibility Prediction" (Hanyang, IEEE Access 2020; 28nm ~800MHz ~10mW predictor vs 1–1.5W compressor).
- **Claimable novelty**: a **measured-parameter profitability-frontier gate** (link-bottleneck B vs alpha, chunk size, decompress ceiling, and per-WR transform-inverse cost) implemented in NIC-path FPGA hardware for bit-exact KV transfer — no one has that; the patent line gates on congestion/link-load heuristics, not on measured codec/engine frontiers, and none is FPGA-validated on LLM tensors.

### Q3 — Three nearest attack-surface papers, exact eval setups, and counters
1. **ShadowServe (arXiv 2509.16857)** — *"SmartNIC KV-cache decompression is already done."* Eval: **real BF3 DPU, but ONE machine** (L40S, CX-7 400G rate-limited to emulate <= 20 Gbps; PCIe 4.0). Counters: (a) lossy (vector-quant before deflate) vs our bit-exact; (b) receive/fetch side of prefix caching vs our sender-side PD-transfer compression; (c) no compression hardware and no gate — deflate encode is software off the critical path; (d) their <= 20 Gbps win region *is* our measured frontier — cite it as independent confirmation, not competition.
2. **NetZIP (MICRO 2025, DOI 10.1145/3725843.3756079)** — *"In-network lossless compression on an FPGA NIC is already done."* Eval: **FPGA-NIC prototype without an RDMA stack (payload-shrinking emulation); 35% training-time headline from SimAI simulation**; LZ4/Snappy; training gradients/activations. Counters: (a) not KV, not inference; (b) not commodity-decodable (both ends custom); (c) gate flag-driven, not data-driven; (d) never faces the RDMA verbs contract (dual-length accounting, placement, CQE) — our contribution surface; (e) its hardware-validation depth (no network stack, sim headline) is *below* what a single VCU118 with a real deflate+transform+gate datapath demonstrates.
3. **TRACE / CXL-NDP (IEEE TC April 2026, arXiv 2509.03377)** — *"Channel-major bit-plane transform + commodity codec + bypass in hardware is already done."* Eval: **DRAMSim3 simulation + 7 nm RTL synthesis (5.7 mm² @ 2 TB/s) — no FPGA, no board, no network**. Counters: (a) CXL memory tier, zero network/NIC content ("No mention of NIC or network transfer"); (b) our transform is constrained to what a single standard deflate stream + existing BF3 engine can decode, and we price the gap (portable alpha 0.671 vs their 0.53 needing custom silicon); (c) FPGA-validated > synthesized-only for an ISCAS audience.
- Runner-up surfaces to pre-cite: **UCCL-Zip** (real 2-node H200/EFA testbed; strongest testbed of the group; counter = GPU-resident custom ANS decoder, competes for GPU, not commodity-decodable, size-threshold gate only), **SplitZip** (H200 + SGLang/Mooncake RoCE 4x200G; counter = worse ratios than ours at BF16 0.755/E5M2 0.877, custom GPU codec), **CXL-SpecKV** (real Agilex-7 but lossy INT8 first stage, CXL not network), **KVFetcher/llm.265** (GPU media ASIC, video bitstream, needs GPU at both ends).

## 3. Implications for a single-board VCU118 ISCAS eval
- **Community norms support it**: NetZIP's own hardware leg has no RDMA stack and its headline is simulation; ShadowServe is one machine with a rate-limited NIC; KVFetcher emulates 1–40 Gbps; TRACE is simulation+synthesis; only UCCL-Zip/SplitZip use real multi-hundred-Gbps fabrics and they are pure software codecs. An honest framing: "datapath (transform + deflate + gate) validated in hardware on XCVU9P at line rate with measured throughput/latency/LUT/BRAM/URAM; system-level benefit derived from the measured-parameter frontier model, whose transfer physics we cross-checked in simulation (M3) and whose profitable region matches ShadowServe's independently measured <= 20 Gbps window."
- **No CC signals needed**: since no published gate is CC-driven either (patents gate on congestion, but no academic FPGA system does), a gate driven by measured frontier parameters + observed data compressibility sidesteps the missing-CC-signal limitation honestly; state Corundum-class open FPGA NICs implement no CC as a factual constraint.
- **Ratio positioning (all verified numbers)**: ours BF16 0.705 / e5m2 0.704 (BF3-decodable) vs SplitZip BF16 ~0.755 / e5m2 0.877 (custom GPU), UCCL-Zip bf16 ~0.64–0.68 / e5m2 ~0.70 (custom GPU ANS), TRACE ~0.53 (custom CXL silicon), nvCOMP LZ4 on raw BF16 KV 1.019x ratio (~alpha 0.98, i.e., useless without transform).
- **Watch items before submission (2026-10-13)**: KVTC-in-KVBM landing (lossy, storage-side — helps narrative), any BF4 compress-engine announcement at DOCA 3.x GA, LMCache MP-mode lossless SERDE default codecs, and the KVFetcher/llm.265 line gaining a PD-transfer variant.

reports.summary: The best single-VCU118, 3-month ISCAS candidates are the ones that stay transport-less, open-loop, and circuit-centric — everything that needs two nodes, congestion signals, or a full RDMA stack is either infeasible on the given hardware or already saturated at NSDI/OSDI/SIGCOMM. Top pick: a verbs-semantics-preserving inline payload-transform engine for RoCEv2 one-sided WRITEs (RETH/length rewrite + PSN/MSN continuity + ICRC recompute after a size-changing transform) — RoCE parsers/generators and full FPGA stacks (MDPI Electronics 2024, StRoM, RoCE BALBOA, RecoNIC, Coyote-v2) exist, but a transport-less bump-in-the-wire that changes payload size while keeping verbs semantics coherent is unpublished and is exactly WR-ZipGuard's claimed contribution surface vs NetZIP. Second: a 100G streaming entropy-conditioning layout-transform circuit (byte-transpose/channel-major corner-turn with deflate-stream framing) — the mechanism exists in radio-astronomy corner-turns and TRACE's custom CXL silicon, but no NIC-path characterization for compression conditioning exists, and it directly reuses the project's measured alpha results. Third: the first academic FPGA implementation of Google's PSP inline encryption at 100G — PSP is open-source (2022), just landed in Linux 6.18, yet only NVIDIA mlx5 hardware supports it and no FPGA paper exists, while generic AES-GCM/MACsec at 100G is fully saturated (commercial IP + papers since 2010). Fourth: a line-rate KV-block prefix-match engine (in-NIC RadixAttention index) — strongest LLM story; ShadowServe (SmartNIC software) and CXL-SpecKV (FPGA'26) are near but leave the hardened-circuit gap open. Fifth: an Ultra Ethernet packet-trimming response engine on the NIC side — UE spec 1.0/1.0.2 is public, trimming is an optional feature, and NIC-side hardware is scarce, though spec churn is a risk. Explicitly rejected as saturated or infeasible: PIFO-family schedulers (PIFO/PIEO/BMW-Tree/BBQ/Gearbox/vPIFO/Sifter), AES-GCM/MACsec cores, ML traffic classification (N3IC/Leo/Taurus/FENIX), packet classification/TCAM alternatives (decades of work), RPC/serialization offload (ProtoAcc/Optimus Prime/Dagger/RPCAcc/RpcNIC at MICRO/ASPLOS/HPCA), collective offload (ACCL+/SCENIC, plus multi-endpoint validation impossible on one board), and CXL-NIC hybrids (VCU118's PCIe Gen3 hard blocks cannot do CXL). All top-5 validate on one board via the VCU118's dual QSFP28 cages (port-to-port DAC cable = real 100G link) plus Corundum's free-license CMAC path and native IEEE 1588 timestamping.

# Alternative NIC data-plane ISCAS paper ideas — web-vetted, single VCU118, 3 months

## 0. Platform facts that gate everything (verified)

- **VCU118** = XCVU9P (2.5M logic cells, 6,840 DSPs, ~346 Mb on-chip RAM), **dual QSFP28 cages**, PCIe x16 edge (Gen3 hard blocks), FMC+/FMC ([AMD product page](https://www.amd.com/en/products/adaptive-socs-and-fpgas/evaluation-boards/vcu118.html), [PCBSync review](https://pcbsync.com/xilinx-vcu118/)). The two QSFP28 cages mean a **single-board real 100G link**: one DAC/AOC cable from cage 0 to cage 1 gives MAC-to-MAC traffic through real PHYs — no second host or NIC needed. Fallback: CMAC near-end PMA loopback.
- **Corundum** (open-source 100G NIC, FCCM'20) explicitly supports VCU118; 100G on UltraScale+ uses the Xilinx CMAC with RS-FEC under the **free CMAC license**; native IEEE 1588 PTP timestamping ships in the shell ([GitHub](https://github.com/corundum/corundum), [FCCM'20 paper](https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~snoeren/papers/corundum-fccm20.pdf)). This is the substrate for every candidate below (RecoNIC needs an ERNIC license and targets Alveo U250; Coyote-v2 targets Alveo).
- **CXL is dead on arrival on VCU118**: CXL needs Gen5-class PCIe + CXL IP (Versal Premium / Agilex-I); XCVU9P hard PCIe is Gen3. All CXL-NIC hybrid ideas are killed on hardware grounds, not novelty grounds.
- **ISCAS fit**: dblp confirms ISCAS runs FPGA-accelerator and crypto-circuit papers continuously (e.g., FPGA NN accelerator ISCAS'20; "FPGA-Based Hardware Optimization for Low-Power High-Speed NLM" at [ISCAS 2026](https://dblp.org/db/conf/iscas/iscas2026.html)). Networking-systems papers are rare at ISCAS — so the pitch must be **circuit-first** (area/f_max/power/latency + one application story), which favors small, self-contained datapath engines and disfavors anything requiring closed-loop transport behavior.

Cross-cutting single-board validation recipe (applies to all top-5): host DMAs golden test vectors / pcap replays into an on-chip AXI-Stream traffic generator → DUT circuit → CMAC → QSFP0 → cable → QSFP1 → CMAC → capture DMA back to host → bit-exact diff vs a Python golden model; sustained-rate measurement from CMAC counters; latency from Corundum's PTP timestamps. Everything is open-loop and deterministic — **no congestion-control signals are needed by any ranked candidate** (this was a hard filter).

---

## 1. Candidate-by-candidate vetting

### C1. Verbs-semantics-preserving inline payload-transform engine for RoCEv2 (transport-less "bump-in-the-wire") — RANK 1

- **Circuit built**: parser for Eth/IPv4/UDP/BTH/RETH of one-sided RDMA WRITE (first/middle/last/only), a pluggable size-changing payload transform stage (pass-through, byte-transpose, or compressor stub), **dual-length accounting** (rewrite RETH DMALen / per-packet length), PSN/MSN continuity bookkeeping across a WR, **ICRC recompute** (CRC32 over masked fields — an LFSR/table hybrid at 512b/cycle is the interesting circuit; prior work notes wide-bus ICRC is the hard part), and a gate that forwards untouched packets on a fast path (ordering-safe dual-path pipeline).
- **Single-board validation**: replay real RoCEv2 pcaps (WR-ZipGuard already has golden KV vectors and a Python model) through the QSFP-to-QSFP loop; verify a stock software RoCE model (or rxe) still accepts the rewritten stream; prove 100G sustain and per-packet added latency.
- **Novelty check**: RoCE **parsers/generators are published** — "A High-Performance FPGA-Based RoCE v2 RDMA Packet Parser and Generator", [MDPI Electronics 13(20):4107, 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/13/20/4107); full FPGA RoCE stacks exist: StRoM (EuroSys'20), [TRETS 2022 RoCEv2 implementation](https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3543176), [RecoNIC](https://github.com/Xilinx/RecoNIC) (ERNIC IP, U250), [RoCE BALBOA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20412) (ETH, 2025: full 100G stack, 250 MHz × 512 b ≈ 128 Gb/s, adds AES + ML-DPI services on the datapath), OPTINIC ([arXiv 2512.22743](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.22743), Coyote-v2/U250), and an EuroMLSys'25 [ML-DPI-for-RDMA paper](https://euromlsys.eu/pdf/euromlsys25-6.pdf). Patents cover NIC-side "RDMA write compressed" ([USPTO example](https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/8001278)). **Gap that survives**: nobody publishes a *transport-less* engine that changes payload size mid-flight while keeping verbs semantics (RETH/PSN/ICRC/completion) coherent — BALBOA terminates the full transport; NetZIP (per WR-ZipGuard's own full-text verification) sits upstream of the protocol engine and never faces the verbs contract. This is precisely the project's documented contribution surface. Count of direct competitors: ~0; adjacent full-stack works: ~5.
- **3-month feasibility**: HIGH. No retransmission, no QP state machine, no MTU discovery — just parse/rewrite/CRC/FIFO on Corundum. The riskiest block (wide ICRC) has published techniques.
- **LLM story**: it *is* the WR-ZipGuard gate datapath (M4a/M4b enabler); measured alpha numbers (0.704/0.705/0.73) plug in as the application section.

### C2. 100G streaming entropy-conditioning layout-transform circuit (byte-transpose + channel-major corner-turn + deflate-stream framing) — RANK 2

- **Circuit built**: dual-clock streaming permutation engine: 2-byte SoA de-interleave (bf16) and head_dim-keyed channel-major reorder (fp8), URAM/BRAM ping-pong tiles, plus framing so the output is consumable as ONE standard deflate stream by a commodity decompressor (BlueField-3-compatible). Characterize area, f_max, power, latency vs tile size; show the transform is a pure permutation (bit-exact invertible).
- **Single-board validation**: DMA captured KV tensors (gpt2/Qwen/Llama already captured) through the loop; verify bit-exact inverse; compression ratio measured downstream in software (transform is the circuit claim; ratio numbers already locked: bf16 0.79→0.705, e5m2 0.73→0.704).
- **Novelty check**: corner-turn/transpose circuits are established in radio astronomy correlators at 100G+ ([CHORD F-engine, arXiv 2607.01625](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.01625), [CHIME](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1608.04347) — URAM ping-pong at 100 GbE), and TRACE does channel-major bit-plane layout **in custom CXL-controller silicon** (IEEE TC, arXiv 2509.03377). **Gap**: no NIC-path, commodity-decodable, compression-conditioning layout transform has been characterized as a circuit; the WR-ZipGuard host-CPU measurements (inverse at only ~2 GB/s/thread) provide the motivation data no one else has. Direct competitors: 0; adjacent mechanism papers: ~4 (different domain).
- **3-month feasibility**: VERY HIGH — smallest circuit of the top 5; leaves schedule room to merge with C1 into one paper (transform stage inside the verbs-preserving engine) if desired.
- **LLM story**: strongest possible — it is M4b's forward transform; also quantifies "portable share of TRACE's gain at line rate" (0.80→0.671 of 0.80→0.53).

### C3. First academic FPGA implementation of Google PSP inline encryption at 100G — RANK 3

- **Circuit built**: PSP tx/rx datapath: UDP encapsulation + PSP header/trailer, AES-GCM-128/256 at 512b/cycle (reuse open cores), and PSP's signature feature — **stateless operation via on-NIC key derivation** (SA derived from a master key, no per-connection state tables), crypt-offset handling, virtualization-friendly key rotation.
- **Single-board validation**: encrypt on TX, loop through cable, decrypt on RX, bit-exact + line-rate; interop vectors from the open PSP spec and the new Linux kernel implementation.
- **Novelty check**: **AES-GCM/MACsec/IPsec at 100G is saturated** — IEEE paper as early as [2010](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/5619894/), commercial cores from [Xiphera (10–200 Gbps)](https://xiphera.com/security-protocols/ipsec/), IP Cores, Design Gateway, Microchip, plus a 2023/24 [100G multi-tenant MACsec paper (Bristol)](https://research-information.bris.ac.uk/en/publications/100-gbps-multi-tenant-fpga-based-macsec-aggregation-to-secure-the/). **But PSP specifically has zero academic FPGA implementations**: open-sourced by [Google in 2022](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/announcing-psp-security-protocol-is-now-open-source), [Linux 6.18 just merged support](https://www.phoronix.com/news/PSP-Encryption-Linux-6.18), and per [LWN](https://lwn.net/Articles/980430/) and [kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/networking/psp.html) the only hardware is NVIDIA mlx5; the only academic artifact found is an Edinburgh MSc software thesis. Direct competitors: 0; adjacent (generic AES-GCM): many — the paper must be framed as protocol-datapath novelty (stateless SA derivation circuit), not cipher novelty.
- **3-month feasibility**: HIGH (cipher cores reusable; PSP spec is short, stable, with test vectors).
- **LLM story**: MODERATE — "encrypt east-west KV/parameter traffic at line rate with zero host tax"; composes with the compression narrative (compress-then-encrypt on the same NIC path) but is not intrinsically about LLMs.

### C4. Line-rate KV-block prefix-match engine ("in-NIC RadixAttention index") — RANK 4

- **Circuit built**: hash-chain longest-prefix matcher over token-block hashes (vLLM APC-style block hashing / SGLang radix semantics): pipelined hash unit + multi-way cuckoo/hopscotch tables in URAM + a chain-walker that returns longest cached prefix + block addresses at line rate, with eviction/coherence update port.
- **Single-board validation**: replay real vLLM/SGLang block-hash traces from the host; measure lookups/s, hit latency, and table-update throughput; loopback packet path optional (index can front a simulated remote fetch).
- **Novelty check**: [ShadowServe (arXiv 2509.16857)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.16857) is "the first SmartNIC-accelerated prefix caching system" — but it offloads the **data plane in software across SmartNIC compute resources** (TPOT up to 2.2× lower, TTFT 1.38× in ≤20 Gbps scenarios — note: the same bandwidth-constrained regime WR-ZipGuard's M3 frontier identified); [CXL-SpecKV (FPGA'26)](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/398721089_CXL-SpecKV_A_Disaggregated_FPGA_Speculative_KV-Cache_for_Datacenter_LLM_Serving) is a disaggregated FPGA KV store with compression; KV-Direct (SOSP'17) is a generic FPGA KVS. **Gap**: a hardened line-rate circuit for longest-prefix-of-block-hashes matching (vs. generic exact-match KVS) appears unpublished. Direct competitors: 0 as a circuit; adjacent systems: 3+ and moving fast — highest scoop risk of the top 5.
- **3-month feasibility**: MEDIUM — hash pipelines are well-trodden, but semantics (prefix chains, eviction coherence) + trace tooling makes the schedule tight.
- **LLM story**: STRONGEST pure-LLM narrative (prefix caching is the hottest serving optimization); ISCAS reviewers may however read it as "a hash table" unless the prefix-chain semantics are foregrounded.

### C5. Ultra Ethernet NIC-side packet-trimming response engine — RANK 5

- **Circuit built**: UET PDS header parser + trimmed-frame detector + hardware NACK/control reflection generator + retransmit-hint queue (the receiver-side fast path that makes trimming useful), sized against UE spec 1.0.2.
- **Single-board validation**: replay synthetic trimmed/untrimmed UET sequences through the loop; measure detection-to-NACK latency and line-rate sustain. No CC loop needed — the circuit's contract is per-packet transformational.
- **Novelty check**: trimming itself is implemented in switch hardware ([arXiv 2207.04967](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.04967), NetFPGA/Tofino/P4; NDP lineage) and is an **optional** UE feature (UE switches must only do ECMP+ECN; [sFlow blog](https://blog.sflow.com/2025/09/packet-trimming.html), [UE spec 1.0.2, Jan 2026](https://ultraethernet.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2026/01/UE-Specification-1.0.2-1.pdf)). Full-stack UET hardware only "expected late 2025/early 2026" and mostly "passes packets as valid" ([WWT](https://www.wwt.com/blog/the-future-of-high-performance-networking-ultra-ethernet-explained), [arXiv 2508.08906](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.08906)). NIC-side trimming-response circuits: 0 found. Timeliness is excellent; risk = 560-page spec reading burden + spec churn + reviewers wanting transport context.
- **3-month feasibility**: MEDIUM (scope discipline required).
- **LLM story**: GOOD at the fabric level (UET is the designated AI-fabric transport for exactly the KV/gradient traffic WR-ZipGuard studies).

---

## 2. Candidates vetted and REJECTED (with saturation evidence)

| Candidate | Verdict | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **PIFO/PIEO packet schedulers** | SATURATED | PIFO SIGCOMM'16, PIEO SIGCOMM'19, BMW-Tree SIGCOMM'23, [BBQ NSDI'24](https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi24/presentation/atre) (FPGA, 100G/148.8 Mpps, 100K flows, 32K priorities @300 MHz, [open SystemVerilog](https://github.com/cmu-snap/BBQ)), [vPIFO SIGCOMM'24](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3651890.3672270), Sifter, plus a 2026 arXiv on line-rate dynamic reordering. A 5-page variant cannot beat this lineage. |
| **Hierarchical shapers** | SATURATED | [Gearbox NSDI'22](https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi22/presentation/gao-peixuan) already did the FPGA prototype (U250, 350 MHz, 100GbE line rate >123B pkts, <1% logic, [open source](https://github.com/Gearbox-NSDI/Gearbox_NSDI)); Carousel/Eiffel cover the algorithm space. |
| **AES-GCM / MACsec / IPsec @100G** | SATURATED | 100G AES-GCM on FPGA published in [2010](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/5619894/); commercial cores everywhere (Xiphera, IP Cores, Design Gateway, Microchip); recent papers exist (Bristol MACsec 2023/24). Only the PSP angle (C3) survives. |
| **CRC/ICRC/checksum engines** | COMMODITY | Decades old as standalone circuits; only interesting *inside* C1 (wide-bus ICRC recompute after payload mutation). |
| **ML traffic classification** | SATURATED | [N3IC NSDI'22](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi22-paper-siracusano.pdf), [Leo NSDI'24](https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi24/presentation/jafri) (multi-terabit), Taurus ASPLOS'22, [FENIX 2025](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.14891), 163-Gbps random-forest FPGA, ML-NIC (2024), SmartNIC foundation-model offload (2025). |
| **Packet classification / TCAM alternatives / range matching** | SATURATED (decades) | Bit-vector FPGA engines >520 Mpps, [TSS bit-selecting trees (ToN 2022)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1109/TNET.2022.3181295), [TeRa 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0167926024000166); learned variants (NuevoMatch) active on the software side. Incremental at best. |
| **RPC / (de)serialization offload** | CROWDED by top venues + contested premise | [ProtoAcc MICRO'21](https://sagark.org/assets/pubs/protoacc-micro2021-preprint.pdf), Optimus Prime ASPLOS'20, Dagger ASPLOS'21, [RPCAcc](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.07632), [RpcNIC HPCA'25](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~mgliu/papers/RpcNIC-hpca25.pdf), Cerebros; Google fleet data (only 16.3% of deserialization cycles in the RPC stack) actively undermines NIC placement. A 5-pager would look like a fragment. |
| **Collective-offload datapath (allreduce blocks)** | SATURATED + validation-broken | [ACCL (100G TCP)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9651265/), [ACCL+ OSDI'24](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi24/presentation/he), [SCENIC 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.15128) (200G, stream compute units, offloaded collectives); collectives fundamentally need multiple endpoints — unconvincing on one board. |
| **Erasure-coding NIC offload** | Mid saturation, weak story | FPGA RS-EC decoders published (TVLSI/Cluster Computing 2024); in-network EC exists on switches; no 100G NIC-inline EC paper found, but the LLM-serving tie is thin — a possible backup, not top-5. |
| **INT generation / hardware timestamping** | Mid saturation | [F3 (CoNEXT'24)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3696397) FPGA telemetry coprocessor; INT on U280 adds only ~900 LUTs (i.e., "too easy" as a circuit paper); PTP is commodity (Corundum ships 1588). Better folded into C1 as per-WR dual-length telemetry. |
| **CXL-NIC hybrid / disaggregated-memory NIC** | INFEASIBLE on VCU118 | XCVU9P hard PCIe is Gen3; CXL requires Gen5-class blocks (Versal Premium/Agilex-I). Also CXL-SpecKV (FPGA'26) already stakes the KV+CXL+FPGA flag. |

---

## 3. Ranked top 5 — justification recap

1. **C1 Verbs-preserving inline transform engine** — zero direct competitors, continues the project's locked-in claim ("verbs-semantics gap is our contribution surface vs NetZIP"), highest strategic value, high feasibility, clean single-board proof (bit-exact + 100G sustain + latency), ISCAS-friendly circuit content (wide ICRC, dual-path ordering-safe pipeline, dual-length accounting).
2. **C2 Entropy-conditioning layout transform @100G** — smallest risk, direct reuse of measured alpha (bf16 0.705 / e5m2 0.704) and host-CPU inverse-cost data (2 GB/s) as motivation; novelty defensible vs radio-astronomy corner-turns (different function/co-design) and TRACE (custom silicon, not commodity-decodable). Natural merge partner with C1 if one stronger paper is preferred over two.
3. **C3 PSP @100G FPGA** — verified first-implementation gap in an otherwise saturated crypto space; perfect ISCAS genre; timing tailwind from Linux 6.18 merge; weakest LLM coupling of the top 3 but still composable ("compress-then-encrypt on the NIC path").
4. **C4 In-NIC KV prefix-match engine** — best pure-LLM narrative and genuinely open as a *circuit*, but tight schedule, fast-moving adjacent systems work (ShadowServe, CXL-SpecKV), and a "just a hash table" perception risk at a circuits venue.
5. **C5 UET trimming-response engine** — maximal timeliness (spec public, hardware scarce, trimming optional-and-unimplemented on NICs), but spec bulk/churn and the temptation of scope creep make it the riskiest 3-month bet.

**Strategic note**: C1+C2 together are effectively WR-ZipGuard M4b reborn as a transport-less, single-board ISCAS paper — they convert the project's existing golden vectors, measured alphas, profitability frontier, and NetZIP-defusal analysis into the application/motivation sections, so ~60% of the paper's non-hardware content already exists.

reports.summary: All four questions verified from AMD/Xilinx primary documents (UG1224 v1.5 PDF pulled from docs.amd.com and text-extracted; DS890 v4.10; PG203 v2.4; AMD product page; Xilinx official dma_ip_drivers readme). (1) The VCU118 has exactly TWO QSFP28 cages (UG1224 calls them "28 Gb/s QSFP+"): QSFP1 U145 wired to all 4 lanes of GTY Quad 231 and QSFP2 U123 to all 4 lanes of GTY Quad 232, each quad with its own independent reference clocks (U38 Si570 156.25 MHz default for Quad 231; U104-buffered Si570 MGT_SI570_CLOCK2 for Quad 232, plus per-quad Si5328B jitter-attenuated clocks) — so simultaneous 2x100G and a one-board port-to-port QSFP28 loopback cable are architecturally supported with no shared-resource conflict. (2) XCVU9P contains 9 hard integrated 100G Ethernet MAC/PCS blocks ("100G Ethernet w/RS-FEC = 9", DS890 Table 15), and PG203's CAUI-4 transceiver-selection rules (4 contiguous GTs from one quad, within an SLR) are exactly satisfied by the full-quad-per-cage wiring, so 2 of the 9 CMACs can drive the two cages at 100G each. (3) PCIe to host is Gen3 x16 on VCU118 Rev 2.0+ (VCCINT=0.85V; pre-Rev-2.0 boards were limited to Gen3 x8); theoretical Gen3 x16 payload ceiling is ~15.75 GB/s/direction and Xilinx's own XDMA readme gives "Maximum data rate for x16 Gen3 is 16Gbytes/s" with a worked measured-efficiency example of 0.78 → 12.48 GB/s, i.e., plan on ~10-13 GB/s realistic streaming. (4) On-board DRAM is two independent 2.5 GB DDR4 80-bit component interfaces (five Micron MT40A256M16GE-083E DDR4-2400 x16 devices each; C1 on HP banks 71-73, C2 on banks 40-42): peak per-channel 19.2 GB/s of 64-bit data (24 GB/s raw over 80 bits incl. ECC lane), ~38.4 GB/s aggregate data bandwidth, plus a 288 MB 72-bit RLD3 interface. Net for the pivot: one VCU118 can host a genuine 2-port 100G hard-MAC loopback link entirely on-board, with host feeding at ~12 GB/s over Gen3 x16 — DDR4 (38 GB/s) will not bottleneck a 2x100G (2x12.5 GB/s) datapath but leaves limited headroom if data crosses DRAM twice.
reports.details:
## (1) QSFP28 cages: TWO, each on its own full GTY quad — 2x100G simultaneous + one-board loopback is supported

**UG1224 (v1.5, March 15, 2023), Ch.3 "28 Gb/s QSFP+ Module Connectors", p.72 (exact quote):**
> "The VCU118 board contains two quad (4-channel) small form-factor pluggable (28 Gb/s QSFP+) connectors, QSFP1 U145 and QSFP2 U123, which accept 28 Gb/s QSFP+ optical modules. Each connector is housed within a single 28 Gb/s QSFP+ cage assembly."

Note the doc's naming: AMD calls them "28 Gb/s QSFP+" — these are QSFP28-class cages (4 lanes x up to 28 Gb/s). The AMD product page lists them as "Two 28 Gb/s QSFP+" / "Two QSFP+ interfaces".

**UG1224 Board Features list, p.7 (exact quotes):**
> "52 GTY transceivers (13 Quads)"
> "2x28 Gb/s QSFP+ connectors (eight GTY transceivers)"
> "PCIe 16-lane edge connector (sixteen GTY transceivers)"
> "FMC+ HSPC connector (twenty-four GTY transceivers)"
> "Samtec Firefly connector (four GTY transceiver)"

**GTY quad wiring (UG1224 "GTY Transceivers" section, pp.58-59, exact quotes):**
> "Four of the GTY transceivers are wired to QSFP1 module connector (U145)"
> "Four of the GTY transceivers are wired to QSFP2 module connector (U123)"
> "Quad 231: MGTREFCLK0 - QSFP_SI570_CLOCK_C_P/N (U38); MGTREFCLK1 - SI5328_CLOCK1_C_P/N (U57); Four GTY transceivers allocated to QSFP1 (U145)"
> "Quad 232: MGTREFCLK0 - MGT_SI570_CLOCK2_C_P/N (U104); MGTREFCLK1 - SI5328_CLOCK2_C_P/N (U57); Four GTY transceivers allocated to QSFP2 (U123)"

Full pin table for QSFP1 = Table 3-22 (MGTYTX/RX[0-3]_231 → U145 pins), QSFP2 = corresponding table for bank 232.

**Independent clocking for simultaneous operation:** Quad 231 REFCLK0 comes from the dedicated U38 Si570 ("QSFP clock 10 MHz-810 MHz, U38 ... oscillator, 156.250 MHz default", Table 3-6); Quad 232 REFCLK0 comes from the U32 Si570 fanned out through the U104 SI53340 buffer (MGT_SI570_CLOCK2, also 156.250 MHz default). Each quad additionally has a Si5328B (U57) jitter-attenuated clock on REFCLK1 (SI5328_CLOCK1 for QSFP1, SI5328_CLOCK2 for QSFP2). So both ports can run 100G at the same time with fully independent reference clocks — nothing is multiplexed between the two cages.

**Verdict:** 2x100G simultaneously = YES (two dedicated 4-lane quads, independent refclks, 9 available hard MACs — see (2)). A QSFP28 direct-attach cable between QSFP1 and QSFP2 creates a real 100G port-to-port link on one board. Caveat to note honestly: UG1224's sentence says the cages "accept 28 Gb/s QSFP+ optical modules"; DAC copper cables are electrically standard QSFP28 and universally used on this board, but UG1224 does not explicitly say "DAC". (The XTP453 quick-start BIST also exercises the QSFP sites with loopback modules.)

## (2) XCVU9P hard CMAC blocks: 9, and they can drive the VCU118 cages

**DS890 "UltraScale Architecture and Product Data Sheet: Overview" (v4.10, May 21, 2026), Table 15 "Virtex UltraScale+ FPGA Feature Summary", pp.14-15 — VU9P column (exact values):**
- 100G Ethernet w/RS-FEC: **9**
- 150G Interlaken: **9**
- PCIE4 (PCIe Gen3 x16): **6**
- GTY Transceivers 32.75 Gb/s: **120**
- System Logic Cells: 2,586,150; CLB LUTs: 1,182,240; DSP: 6,840; Block RAM: 2,160 blocks / 75.9 Mb; UltraRAM: 960 / 270.0 Mb

So the XCVU9P has nine integrated (hard) 100G Ethernet MAC+PCS blocks, each with hard RS-FEC. In Vivado these are the CMACE4 primitives instantiated by the "UltraScale+ Devices Integrated 100G Ethernet Subsystem" IP (PG203): "The core instantiates the UltraScale+ Devices Integrated Block for 100G Ethernet." (PG203 v2.4, Overview, p.5).

**Usable with the QSFP cages?** PG203 v2.4, "Transceiver Selection Rules", p.81 (exact quotes):
> "IMPORTANT: CAUI-4 and switchable CAUI-10/CAUI-4 require GTY transceivers." (p.6)
> "If implementing CAUI-4: CAUI-4 GTs have to be contiguous. CAUI-4 must use GTs from the same horizontal CR or two above or below. CAUI-4 all GTs must come from the same GT quad. CAUI-4 is only supported in Lanes 1-4. CAUI-4 must be implemented within an SLR."

The VCU118 wiring (one full 4-lane GTY quad per cage: 231→QSFP1, 232→QSFP2) satisfies every CAUI-4 rule per cage, and CAUI-4 = 4x25.78125 Gb/s is far below the 32.75 Gb/s GTY ceiling (DS890) for the board's -2 speed-grade device (UG1224: "The XCVU9P-L2FLGA2104 (-2 speed grade) is deployed on the VCU118"). The cmac_usplus IP's Vivado board flow provides VCU118 presets for exactly these two ports (quads 231/232 with the 156.25 MHz U38/U104 refclks). Corroboration (non-official but decisive practice): Corundum's open-source NIC ships a VCU118 target driving BOTH QSFP28 cages at 100G via two CMACE4 instances (github.com/corundum/corundum, device table lists VCU118 / XCVU9P / 2x QSFP28).

**Verdict:** 9 hard CMACs; 2 of them can be bonded to the two QSFP28 cages simultaneously; this is the standard, officially-supported configuration path (cmac_usplus IP + GTY quads 231/232).

## (3) PCIe to host: Gen3 x16 (board Rev 2.0+), realistic streaming ~10-13 GB/s

**UG1224 p.7 Board Features (exact quotes):**
> "PCI Express endpoint connectivity: Gen1 16-lane (x16); Gen2 16-lane (x16); Gen3 8-lane (x8) (Pre-Rev. 2.0 VCU118 board VCCINT = 0.72V); Gen3 16-lane (x16) (VCU118 Rev. 2.0 and later VCCINT = 0.85V)"

**UG1224 "PCI Express Endpoint Connectivity", p.67 (exact quotes):**
> "The 16-lane PCI Express edge connector U2 performs data transfers at the rate of 2.5 GT/s for Gen1 applications, 5.0 GT/s for Gen2 applications, and 8.0 GT/s for Gen3 applications."
> "On VCU118 Rev. 2.0 and later boards, VCCINT = 0.85V and PCIe Gen 3 x16 is supported." (footnote p.~4796 of extracted text: "PCI Express Gen3 x16 operation is not supported when VCCINT = 0.72V.")

The device provides 6 hard PCIE4 blocks (DS890 Table 15), one of which is wired to the x16 edge connector via GTY quads 224-227 (UG1224 GTY section: "Sixteen of the GTY transceivers are wired to the PCIe 16-lane edge connector (U2)").

**Realistic streaming bandwidth (official Xilinx numbers):** theoretical Gen3 x16 = 8 GT/s x 16 x 128b/130b ≈ 15.75 GB/s per direction. Xilinx's official XDMA driver documentation (Xilinx/dma_ip_drivers, XDMA/linux-kernel/readme.txt) states verbatim:
> "Maximum data rate for x16 Gen3 is 16Gbytes/s"
> "for a x16Gen3 design value of 0.78 data rate is 0.78*16 = 12.48Gbytes/s" (and for x8 Gen3: "0.81*8 = 6.48Gbytes/s")

AMD's formal measured tables are in AR68049 ("DMA Subsystem for PCI Express - Performance Numbers", referenced by the official PCIe Debug K-Map as the performance source), which is JS-gated and could not be scraped; community-reported XDMA figures on Gen3 x16 cluster at ~10-13 GB/s. Planning number: **~12 GB/s H2C/C2H sustained with XDMA/QDMA at Gen3 x16; half that (~6.5 GB/s) if the slot/bifurcation drops to x8.**

## (4) On-board DRAM: 2 x 2.5 GB DDR4-2400, 80-bit each (~38 GB/s aggregate data BW) + 288 MB RLD3

**UG1224 p.7 Board Features (exact quote):**
> "Two 2.5 GB DDR4 80-bit component memory interfaces (five [256 Mb x 16] devices each)"
> "288 MB 72-bit RLD3 memory interface comprised of two 1.125 Gb 36-bit devices"

**UG1224 "DDR4 Component Memory", pp.21-22 (exact quotes):**
> "The DDR4 component memory system is comprised of two 2.5 GB sets of five 256 Mb x 16 (80-bit wide) DDR4 SDRAM devices, U60-U64 (C1) and U135-U139 (C2)."
> "Manufacturer: Micron; Part Number: MT40A256M16GE-083E; 4 Gb (256 Mb x 16); 1.2V 96-ball TFBGA; DDR4-2400"
> "This dual memory system is connected in 80-bit wide interfaces to the U1 XCVU9P HP banks 71, 72, 73 (C1) and 40, 41, 42 (C2)."

**Derived bandwidth (arithmetic, not a doc quote):** each channel at DDR4-2400 (-083E part = 2400 MT/s): 64-bit data payload → 19.2 GB/s peak; full 80-bit lane width (64 data + 16 typically used as ECC in MIG) → 24.0 GB/s raw. Two independent channels → **38.4 GB/s peak data bandwidth (48 GB/s raw)**; expect ~70-85% efficiency with MIG for streaming patterns. Capacity: 5 GB total raw (2 x 2.5 GB); if MIG is configured 64-bit+ECC, usable data capacity is 2 x 2 GB. DS923 (Virtex UltraScale+ DC/AC switching, docs.amd.com/r/en-US/ds923-virtex-ultrascale-plus) caps DDR4 component PHY rate at 2666 Mb/s for top grades — the board's 2400 MT/s devices are the binding limit, not the FPGA.

## Implications for the pivot (facts only, from the above)
- One VCU118 = a real 2-port 100G link: CMAC0(quad 231, QSFP1) ↔ DAC ↔ CMAC1(quad 232, QSFP2), both hard MACs, RS-FEC in silicon, one board. This is architecturally identical to a NIC egress + NIC ingress pair.
- Rate budget: 100G line rate = 12.5 GB/s; PCIe Gen3 x16 realistic ~12 GB/s just barely feeds ONE 100G port from host at line rate; DDR4 38.4 GB/s peak can source/sink both ports once, but a store-and-forward architecture that writes+reads DRAM per direction (2x100G x 2 = 50 GB/s) would exceed it — plan on streaming through URAM/BRAM (270 Mb UltraRAM available) or single-DRAM-touch designs.
- Board Rev matters: confirm the physical board is Rev 2.0 or later (VCCINT 0.85V) for Gen3 x16; pre-Rev-2.0 is Gen3 x8 only (~6.5 GB/s).

reports.summary: Corundum is the only one of the four options with first-class VCU118 support: its README lists "Xilinx VCU118 (Xilinx Virtex UltraScale+ XCVU9P)" and the official device list documents 2x QSFP28 with three design variants (2x100G via CMAC, 2x25G, 2x10G) on PCIe Gen3 x16 — but the repo is dormant (master tip Dec 2, 2023; last push to any branch 2024-07-05; no releases), so treat it as a stable-but-unmaintained substrate. ETH Coyote v2 does NOT support VCU118 — the README names only "AMD Alveo U55C, U250, U280 and, recently, V80 (currently without networking)" — although it does ship a working 100G RoCE-v2 RDMA stack (example 09_perf_rdma) and is very actively maintained (pushed 2026-07-14, the day of this search). AMD OpenNIC shell supports only Alveo boards (U50/U55N/U55C/U200/U250/U280/U45N); VCU118 appears nowhere in the README or the build script's -board values, and the repo's last push was 2025-01-02. AMD ERNIC IP is device-compatible with the XCVU9P (IP Facts lists Virtex UltraScale+; 100 Gb/s data path, up to 255 QPs) but is encrypted RTL with no testbench/simulation model, license-gated at synthesis/implementation/write_bitstream, priced at $92,400 for a 1-year site license (DigiKey EF-DI-ERNIC-SITE), with the academic route being an AMD University Program application (per Xilinx's own RecoNIC README) — and its reference shell (RecoNIC) targets Alveo U250, not VCU118. Net assessment for the 3-month ISCAS plan: Corundum's VCU118 fpga_100g design is the realistic integration target; Coyote/OpenNIC would each require a board port that is out of scope; ERNIC is not realistically usable in 3 months (license lead time + encrypted RTL + U250-only reference design + no second node to exercise RDMA anyway).

## (1) Corundum — VCU118 supported, repo dormant since mid-2024

**VCU118 support (primary source, README.md):** The board list of example designs includes the exact line:
> "Xilinx VCU118 (Xilinx Virtex UltraScale+ XCVU9P)"

**Port configuration (primary source, docs.corundum.io device list):** the VCU118 entry reads:
- "FPGA: XCVU9P-L2FLGA2104E", "Board ID: 0x10ee9076"
- "PCIe IF: Gen 3 x16"
- "Network IF: 2x QSFP28"
- "DDR: 4 GB DDR4 2666 (2x 256M x80)"
- Three design variants, all with "2x1" interface/port configuration and 256/8K RXQ/TXQ:
  1. `mqnic/fpga_100g/fpga` — 100G per port (i.e., **2x100G**)
  2. `mqnic/fpga_25g/fpga` — 25G per port (2x25G)
  3. `mqnic/fpga_25g/fpga_10g` — 10G per port (2x10G)

**100G design details (primary source, `fpga/mqnic/VCU118/fpga_100g/README.md`):** FPGA part "xcvu9p-flga2104-2L-e"; PHY: "100G CAUI-4 CMAC and internal GTY transceivers"; MAC: "Xilinx 100G CMAC". Standard flow: `make` in fpga dir for bitstream, `modules/mqnic` kernel driver, `utils` userspace tools. Design directories `fpga_25g/` and `fpga_100g/` confirmed present under `fpga/mqnic/VCU118/` on GitHub.

**Activity 2025-2026 (primary source, GitHub API + commits page):**
- `pushed_at: 2024-07-05T08:24:12Z` (any branch); newest commits on master dated **Dec 2, 2023** (e.g., "merged changes in eth"); a Nov 29, 2023 commit even touches VCU118: "Add user_sma_clk pins to VCU108 and VCU118 constraints files".
- 2,394 stars, 542 forks, 130 open issues, **no published releases**, default branch `master`.
- Verdict: **zero code activity in 2025-2026** — dormant ~2 years as of 2026-07-14. Feature set per README: "high performance datapath, 10G/25G/100G Ethernet, PCI express gen 3, a custom, high performance, tightly-integrated PCIe DMA engine", "many (1000+) transmit, receive, completion, and event queues", included Linux driver. No RDMA/RoCE stack (plain Ethernet NIC) — consistent with the project constraint that no transport CC signals are available.

## (2) ETH Coyote v2 — Alveo-only, no VCU118; yes, working 100G RoCE stack; very active

**Board support (primary source, README.md, exact line):**
> "Coyote supports the following FPGA platforms: AMD Alveo U55C, U250, U280 and, recently, V80 (currently without networking)."

No mention of VCU118 or any Virtex UltraScale+ dev board anywhere in the README. Prerequisites: "For UltraScale+ devices (U55c, U250, U280), Coyote requires Vivado 2022.1 or newer"; "For Versal devices (V80), Coyote requires Vivado 2024.2 or newer".

**RoCE stack (primary source, README + examples/):**
> "Networking services: 100G RoCE-v2 compatible RDMA, TCP/IP and collectives"

Example `09_perf_rdma` is described as: "Using the FPGA as a SmartNIC for Remote Direct Memory Access: How to do networking with Coyote's internal, 100G, fully RoCEv2-compliant networking stack." (Networking examples are marked not yet supported on V80.) So yes — a shipped, exercised 100G RoCE-v2 stack, but only on Alveo U55C/U250/U280.

**Activity (GitHub API):** `pushed_at: 2026-07-14T04:47:18Z` (same day as this search), 424 stars, 111 forks, 12 open issues, default branch `master`. Coyote v2 paper: "Coyote v2: Raising the Level of Abstraction for Data Center FPGAs".

**Implication:** porting Coyote's shell (built around Alveo platforms/HBM) to VCU118 is a board-port project in itself — out of scope for 3 months.

## (3) AMD OpenNIC shell — VCU118 NOT included

**Board list (primary source, README.md, exact lines):**
> "- Xilinx Alveo U50, - Xilinx Alveo U55N, - Xilinx Alveo U55C, - Xilinx Alveo U200, - Xilinx Alveo U250, - Xilinx Alveo U280, - Xilinx Alveo U45N"

"VCU118 is not mentioned anywhere" in the README. The build script's `-board` valid values are: `au250, au280, au200, au55c, au55n, au50, U45N`. Vivado requirement: "The latest version is built with Vivado 2020.x, 2021.x or 2022.1." (note: "Vivado 2022.2 uses QDMA v5.0", driver may need upgrading).

**Activity (GitHub API):** `pushed_at: 2025-01-02T19:58:15Z`, 145 stars, 90 forks, 25 open issues, default branch `main`. Maintenance mode; one release tag. The parent open-nic overview describes the shell as supporting "up to four PCI-e physical functions (PFs) and two 100Gbps Ethernet ports" — but only on the listed Alveo cards. A web search for VCU118 ports/forks of open-nic-shell found none (only the esnet mirror fork, same board list).

## (4) AMD ERNIC IP — device-compatible, but license-gated, encrypted, expensive, U250-referenced: not realistic in 3 months

**Device support (primary source, PG332 v3.0 PDF, IP Facts table, read directly):**
> "Supported Device Family: Kintex UltraScale+, Virtex UltraScale, Virtex UltraScale+, Zynq UltraScale+"
> Note 3: "For UltraScale devices, only 40G data path is supported."

(The current docs.amd.com PG332 v4.x IP Facts adds "AMD Versal Adaptive SoC".) The **XCVU9P on VCU118 is Virtex UltraScale+, so it is in the supported device family** — but AMD ships **no VCU118 board-level reference design**; the ERNIC ecosystem reference (RecoNIC) targets Alveo U250.

**Key specs (PG332 v3.0, exact lines):** "100 Gb/s data path"; "Designed to scale up to 255 RDMA Queue pairs" with the note "Default Vivado strategies allow for the timing to pass up to 127 queue pairs"; "Support for up to 254 connections"; RC transport; "Supports incoming and outgoing RDMA SEND, RDMA READ, RDMA WRITE, RDMA SEND WITH IMM, RDMA WRITE WITH IMM, and RDMA SEND WITH INVALIDATE"; "Atomic operations are not supported"; ECN and PFC supported; "The ERNIC IP interfaces with any Ethernet MAC IP using an AXI4-Stream interface" (512-bit internal datapath; MAC/CMAC NOT included — pair it with the free UltraScale+ CMAC hard block).

**Deliverables (IP Facts):** Design files: "Encrypted RTL"; Example design: Verilog; **"Test Bench: Not Provided"; "Simulation Model: Not Provided."**

**License model (PG332 v3.0, Licensing and Ordering, exact text):**
> "This Xilinx LogiCORE IP module is provided under the terms of the Xilinx Core License Agreement. The module is shipped as part of the Vivado Design Suite. For full access to all core functionalities in simulation and in hardware, you must purchase a license for the core... Evaluation licenses and hardware timeout licenses might be available for this core or subsystem. Contact your local Xilinx sales representative for information about pricing and availability."

License checkers gate "Vivado synthesis, Vivado implementation, write_bitstream (Tcl command)" — you cannot even produce a bitstream without a valid license.

**Price (primary source, DigiKey product page for EF-DI-ERNIC-SITE):** **$92,400.00**, described as "DEV RNIC SITE LICENSE", "License 1 Year Site", electronically delivered.

**Academic route (primary source, Xilinx/RecoNIC README, exact line):**
> "ERNIC license is required in this project. You can either purchase or apply for it through AMD University Program."

RecoNIC itself (Xilinx's open shell integrating ERNIC): targets "AMD-Xilinx Alveo U250" (two servers connected via 100G), requires Vivado 2021.2; 174 stars, 58 commits, maintenance mode.

**3-month realism verdict: NO.** Four compounding blockers: (a) license acquisition — either $92.4k or an AMD University Program application with uncertain approval lead time; (b) encrypted RTL with no testbench/sim model makes debugging and modification (e.g., inserting a compression stage in the TX path) essentially impossible; (c) the only public reference integration (RecoNIC) is U250-based, so a VCU118 port of the shell/driver stack would be needed on top; (d) with exactly one host and no second NIC, an RDMA NIC cannot demonstrate any end-to-end behavior anyway — the license would buy nothing measurable for the ISCAS paper.

## Comparison table

| Shell | VCU118? | Port config | RoCE/RDMA | Activity (as of 2026-07-14) | License |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Corundum | **YES** (first-class) | 2x QSFP28: 2x100G (CMAC), 2x25G, 2x10G; PCIe Gen3 x16 | No (plain NIC) | Dormant: master Dec 2023, push 2024-07-05, 2.4k stars | BSD-ish open source |
| Coyote v2 | NO (U55C/U250/U280/V80) | 100G on Alveo | **Yes, 100G RoCE-v2 + example** | Very active: pushed 2026-07-14 | Open source |
| OpenNIC shell | NO (7 Alveo boards) | 2x100G on Alveo | No | Slow: pushed 2025-01-02 | Open source (AMD) |
| ERNIC IP | Device family yes (Virtex US+), board reference no (U250 via RecoNIC) | 100 Gb/s datapath, MAC not included | Yes (RoCEv2 hard-offload, no atomics) | PG332 v4.3 current; RecoNIC maintenance mode | **$92,400/yr site (DigiKey); encrypted RTL; XUP application for academics** |

**Bottom line for the pivot:** the only VCU118-native NIC substrate is Corundum's `fpga/mqnic/VCU118/fpga_100g` (2x100G CMAC) design — dormant but complete, with Linux driver and a clean AXI-Stream datapath where a byte-transpose/channel-reorder + deflate TX pipeline stage could be inserted. None of the four gives you RoCE on VCU118 within 3 months, which is consistent with the stated constraint (no transport modification, no two-node link).

reports.summary: YES — 3-6 GB/s deflate compression on a VU9P alongside a NIC shell is realistic, with three independent lines of primary-source evidence. (1) AMD's Vitis Data Compression Library officially benchmarks its GZip/Zlib compress kernel at 2 GB/s per compute unit at 300 MHz on Alveo U200 (same XCVU9P-class die as the VCU118), with compression ratio 2.70 on Silesia, costing only ~54K LUT / ~141 BRAM / 64 URAM per CU (~4.6% / 6.5% / 6.7% of a VU9P), and the docs explicitly state there is room for more CUs; 2-3 CUs gives 4-6 GB/s for under ~14% LUT / ~20% URAM. (2) Academic: Ledwon & Cockburn (IEEE Access 2020) achieved a fixed 4.0 GB/s deflate compress at 250 MHz on the much smaller XCVU3P (~17.5% of its LUTs, i.e. ~6% of a VU9P), and Fowers et al. (FCCM 2015, Microsoft) hit 5.6 GB/s on a 28nm Stratix V with ~100K ALMs — both far below VU9P capacity. (3) Commercial: CAST's ZipAccel-C press release states ">90 Gbps" (~11 GB/s) compression on the Alveo U200, and its product page claims >100 Gbps feasible in FPGAs generally. Against this, the Corundum 100G NIC shell on VCU118 uses only ~62K LUT (5%) / 331 BRAM (15%) / 20 URAM (2%), so compressor + NIC together stay under ~20% LUT / ~35% BRAM of the VU9P. The two real risks are (a) compression-ratio degradation: hardware deflate ratios are 1.92-2.70 on text corpora (Vitis 2.70 Silesia beats zlib -1 but trails zlib -6 ~3.1; Ledwon's static-Huffman 1.92 Calgary is notably weaker), so WR-ZipGuard's α≈0.70-0.73 measured with software zlib must be re-verified against the specific hardware encoder configuration on KV bytes; and (b) engineering risk of SLR-crossing timing closure at 300 MHz and DMA plumbing between the NIC datapath and the compressor, not raw throughput or area.
reports.details:
## 1. AMD Vitis Data Compression Library — official benchmark (primary source)

Benchmark page (2021.2, identical numbers persist in the master GitHub README as of 2026): measured on **Alveo U200** (XCU200 = Virtex UltraScale+ VU9P-class die, same family/size as the VCU118's XCVU9P) on the **Silesia corpus**.

### Compression table (quoted rows, per single compute unit)

| Architecture | Block Size | Comp. Ratio | Throughput | FMax | LUT | BRAM | URAM |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GZip/Zlib 32KB Memory Mapped | 32KB | 2.70 | 2 GB/s | 300MHz | 57K | 135 | 64 |
| GZip 32KB Compress Stream | 32KB | 2.70 | 2 GB/s | 300MHz | 54K | 141 | 64 |
| Zlib 32KB Compress Stream | 32KB | 2.70 | 2 GB/s | 300MHz | 54K | 128 | 64 |
| GZip Fixed 32KB Compress Stream (fixed Huffman) | 32KB | 2.31 | 2 GB/s | 300MHz | 35K | 45 | 64 |
| Zlib Fixed 32KB Compress Stream | 32KB | 2.31 | 2 GB/s | 300MHz | 35.7K | 39 | 64 |
| Zstd Compress Quad Core | 32KB | 2.68 | 1.17 GB/s | 284MHz | 40K | 79 | 37 |

### Decompression (for contrast — confirms compress/decompress asymmetry)

| Architecture | Throughput | FMax | LUT | BRAM | URAM |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GZip/Zlib Streaming (full standard: dynamic+fixed+stored) | 518 MB/s | 283MHz | 6.7K | 8 | 0 |

### Key quoted statements
- Kernel detail page (2022.1, L2 gzipc): "The final Fmax achieved is 300MHz", "Compression Throughput 2 GB/s", "Average Compression Ratio 2.70x (Silesia Benchmark)"; resource row: LUT 54K, LUTMem 7.7K, REG 48.7K, BRAM 141, URAM 64.
- CPU comparison (README/benchmark): "19.3x speedup using single GZIP compress kernel against single core CPU Zlib fast (1.2.11, -1)".
- Multi-CU headroom (benchmark page): resource utilization "indicates remaining capacity on Alveo U200 for additional compute units to further boost throughput" (paraphrased from page; original: the resources used indicate there is still room on Alveo U200 for more compute units to further improve throughput).

### Multi-CU arithmetic on VU9P (from DS890 v4.10, May 2026: VU9P = 1,182,240 LUTs; 2,364,480 FFs; 2,160 BRAM blocks / 75.9 Mb; 960 URAM / 270 Mb)
- 1 CU = 2 GB/s: 54K LUT (4.6%), 141 BRAM (6.5%), 64 URAM (6.7%)
- 2 CUs = 4 GB/s: ~108K LUT (9.1%), ~282 BRAM (13.1%), 128 URAM (13.3%)
- 3 CUs = 6 GB/s: ~162K LUT (13.7%), ~423 BRAM (19.6%), 192 URAM (20.0%)

Note: multi-CU parallelism is block-level (32KB blocks / separate streams per CU) — compatible with WR-ZipGuard's >=256KB per-WR chunking, but chunks must be split across CUs or CUs fed with independent WRs.

## 2. Published UltraScale+/VU9P-relevant deflate ENCODER results

### Ledwon & Cockburn (+ Han), IEEE Access 8 (2020) 62207-62217, DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2020.2984191
- Vivado HLS, **Xilinx Virtex UltraScale+ XCVU3P-FFVC1517** (same 16nm UltraScale+ fabric as VU9P; VU3P has exactly 1/3 the LUTs: 394,080 vs 1,182,240).
- Abstract: "The proposed compressor processes data at a fixed input throughput of 4.0 GB/s and achieves a geometric mean compression ratio of 1.92" (Calgary corpus, static Huffman; 250 MHz, 16-byte parallel word).
- Utilization on XCVU3P: **17.54% LUT** (~69K), 6.31% FF, 36.18% BRAM (~260 of 720 blocks). Scaled to VU9P that is ~5.8% LUT / ~12% BRAM.
- Claimed "25% greater throughput and an 11% greater compression ratio than the only other published design that uses Vivado HLS."
- Thesis (Univ. of Alberta, M. Ledwon, "Design of FPGA-based Accelerators for Deflate Compression and Decompression using High-Level Synthesis") confirms device and numbers.

### Fowers, Kim, Burger, Hauck (Microsoft), FCCM 2015 — "A Scalable High-Bandwidth Architecture for Lossless Compression on FPGAs" (verbatim Table I, Calgary corpus, Stratix V @ 175 MHz)

| Design | Perf. (GB/s) | Comp. Ratio | Area (ALMs) | Efficiency (MB/s/kALM) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ZLIB (fastest) | 0.038 | 2.62 | N/A | N/A |
| IBM | 4 | 2.17 | 110,000* | 38 |
| Altera (OpenCL) | 4 | 2.17 | 123,000* | 33 |
| PWS=16 | 2.8 | 1.93 | 35,115 | 80 |
| PWS=16 w/ HT | 2.8 | 2.05 | 39,078 | 72 |
| PWS=32 | 5.6 | 1.97 | 100,754 | 56 |
| PWS=32 w/ HT | 5.6 | 2.09 | 108,350 | 52 |

(*extrapolated by the authors.) Quote: scaling "to 5.6 GB/s of throughput... our architecture achieves the highest throughput and area-efficiency of any published high-bandwidth FPGA compressor" (at time of writing). This is 28nm silicon at 175 MHz — a 16nm VU9P at 250-300 MHz has both more fabric and more speed headroom. Paper also cites IBM 4 GB/s (Sukhwani et al., FCCM) and the AHA378 PCIe product "capable of up to 10GB/s".

### CAST ZipAccel-C (commercial IP, sold through AMD/Xilinx IP catalog)
- Product page (cast-inc.com, retrieved via search index; direct fetch 403s): "Throughputs in excess of 100 Gbps are feasible even in low-cost FPGAs, and latency can be as small as a few tens of clock cycles"; ASIC-oriented claim: "over 400 Gbps... feasible at clock rates as low as 500MHz". Performance "can scale by instantiating more search engines and/or Huffman encoders"; ratio/throughput/latency tunable via search-window options.
- Press release (2019, via design-reuse.com): "data compression at over 90 Gigabits per second (Gbps) is possible with the compression IP running on the mid-range Alveo U200 Card" — i.e. **>11 GB/s deflate compress demonstrated commercially on the same VU9P-class die** as the VCU118.

## 3. NIC-shell coexistence budget (Corundum, FCCM 2020, "Corundum: An Open-Source 100-Gbps NIC")
Corundum officially supports the VCU118. Reported utilization on VCU118 (XCVU9P), 100G configuration: **62.4K LUTs (5%), 76.8K FFs (3%), 331 BRAMs (15%), 20 URAMs (2%)** (10G config: 70.0K LUT/252 BRAM). 100G on UltraScale+ uses the hard CMAC with RS-FEC.

**Combined budget check (VU9P):** Corundum 100G shell + 3 Vitis GZip CUs (6 GB/s) ≈ 224K LUT (19%), ~754 BRAM (35%), 212 URAM (22%) — leaves >60% of the device free. Even adding CAST-class IP at 90 Gbps was demonstrated on U200 *with* the Alveo XDMA shell present.

## 4. Verdict on the assigned question
**YES — 3-6 GB/s deflate compress on the VCU118's XCVU9P alongside a NIC shell is realistic**, supported independently by (a) AMD's own 2 GB/s/CU @ 300 MHz benchmark on the same die class with explicit multi-CU headroom, (b) a peer-reviewed 4.0 GB/s HLS design that fits in one-third-of-VU9P silicon, (c) Microsoft's 5.6 GB/s on older 28nm silicon, and (d) CAST selling >90 Gbps (>11 GB/s) on Alveo U200. Resource arithmetic closes with large margin against Corundum's measured 5% LUT / 15% BRAM shell cost.

**Caveats to carry into the paper/plan:**
1. **Ratio-throughput tradeoff is the binding constraint, not speed.** High-throughput encoders weaken match search: Vitis dynamic-Huffman = 2.70 Silesia (vs software zlib -6 ≈ 3.1; their own baseline comparison is zlib **-1**); Vitis fixed-Huffman = 2.31; Ledwon static-Huffman = 1.92 Calgary; Fowers = 1.97-2.09. WR-ZipGuard's locked α (0.704-0.73 fp8, 0.705 bf16-transposed) was measured with *software* zlib — the hardware encoder's α on transformed KV bytes must be re-measured (HLS csim/cosim of the Vitis kernel is sufficient and needs no second host). Since much of the KV win is entropy coding of the exponent plane, dynamic-Huffman variants (2.70-class) are the right choice; fixed-Huffman variants would likely cost α.
2. **Throughput needed vs link math:** to keep a bottleneck link B saturated with compressed data, compressor input rate ≈ B/α. At α≈0.73: B=20 Gbps → 3.4 GB/s input; B=40 Gbps → 6.8 GB/s. So 2-3 CUs (4-6 GB/s) covers the profitable region identified by M3 (B_crit ≈ 20-60 Gbps at the FPGA-sender scenarios), and one CU (2 GB/s) already covers B ≤ ~11-12 Gbps.
3. **Engineering risks:** SLR-crossing timing closure on the 3-SLR VU9P at 300 MHz (mitigate by pinning CUs per SLR — the U200 benchmark already closes 300 MHz with a shell present); integrating the forward transform (byte-transpose/channel-major) upstream of the compressor is cheap (pure permutation, trivially streamable in fabric); per-CU block-level parallelism requires feeding CUs with independent >=32KB blocks, consistent with the >=256KB chunk constraint from M2.
4. **Source-access notes:** cast-inc.com and its datasheet PDFs return 403 to non-browser fetchers; CAST quotes above come from the search-indexed product page text and the design-reuse mirror of the official press release. IEEE Xplore blocked full-text for Ledwon; numbers were cross-confirmed from the Semantic Scholar abstract record, the University of Alberta thesis record, and search-indexed excerpts of the paper's tables.

## 1. Is 2026-10-13 the correct deadline? — YES, CONFIRMED FROM THE OFFICIAL ISCAS 2027 CFP

The ISCAS 2027 Call for Papers is live at https://2027.ieee-iscas.org/call-for-papers. Exact quoted lines from that page:

| Item | Exact CFP line |
|---|---|
| Special sessions | "Special Session Proposal Deadline: September 11, 2026" |
| **Regular papers** | **"Regular Paper Submission Deadline: October 13, 2026"** |
| Tutorials | "Tutorial Proposal Deadline: October 13, 2026" |
| Live demos | "Live Demonstration Submission Deadline: October 13, 2026" |
| Notification | "Author Notification: January 11, 2027" |
| Camera-ready | "Final Paper Submission: January 27, 2027" |

So from today (2026-07-14) there are exactly 91 days to the regular-paper deadline.

## 2. Conference dates / location

Official homepage (https://2027.ieee-iscas.org/): "BORDEAUX - FRANCE | 6-9 JUNE 2027" and "ISCAS 2027 will be held in Bordeaux, France, from 6 to 9 June 2027". Flagship conference of the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society (CASS); CCF rank B.

## 3. Page limit — 5 pages total, but only 4 for technical content (references-only 5th page)

- The ISCAS 2027 CFP page does **not** yet state a regular-paper page limit, and no 2027 author-instructions page exists yet (https://2027.ieee-iscas.org/authors/author-instructions.html returns 404). This is the one item where the prior year is the proxy — stated explicitly per task instructions.
- ISCAS **2026** author instructions (https://2026.ieee-iscas.org/authors/author-instructions.html), exact quote: "Maximum 5 pages, of which 4 are for technical content including text, figures and references (if any), and with one additional optional 5th page containing only references".
- ISCAS **2025** initial author instructions (https://2025.ieee-iscas.org/initial-author-instructions/) contain the **identical sentence**, and search results indicate ISCAS 2024 used the same wording — this rule has been stable for at least three consecutive years and is overwhelmingly likely to apply to 2027.
- Practical implication for the writing plan: budget **4 pages** for abstract + all text + all figures/tables; references go on an optional 5th page (references may also sit inside the 4 pages "if any", but nothing except references may appear on page 5).
- Other format constraints (2025/2026): PDF, max 5 MB, US Letter or A4, all fonts embedded, no Type 3 fonts, no PDF security; "Deviations from the above paper specifications could impede the review of your paper and result in rejection."
- Review policy: **single-blind**. ISCAS 2026: "ISCAS is NOT double-blind review this year. Please include author information on your submission." ISCAS 2025: "Reviews will be single-blind." No anonymization needed (assume same for 2027 unless the 2027 author instructions later say otherwise — worth a re-check ~September 2026 when they post).

## 4. Submission categories (from the 2027 CFP, exact quotes)

- "Regular Papers: original research contributions to the state-of-the-art in circuits and systems."
- Special Sessions: "Proposal should include the following information (3 pages max.)" — proposals due September 11, 2026 (an alternative path if a themed session on AI-infrastructure circuits exists).
- Tutorials: "The proposal should include a two-page (maximum) description".
- Live Demonstrations: "Authors are invited to submit a one-page demo description", using "the same page formatting as for regular ISCAS papers" — a VCU118 board demo is exactly the kind of artifact this category wants, and it shares the October 13, 2026 deadline.

## 5. Track list (complete, verbatim from the ISCAS 2027 CFP) — with fit assessment

1. Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuits and Systems
2. **Digital Integrated Circuits and Systems** — natural home for an FPGA deflate/transform datapath implementation
3. Power and Energy Circuits and Systems
4. Sensory Circuits and Systems
5. Nonlinear Systems and Circuit Theory
6. **Digital Signal Processing** — plausible for the byte-transpose/channel-major transform pipeline
7. Multimedia Systems and Applications
8. **Communications Circuits and Systems** — fits the NIC-path / link-bottleneck framing
9. Biomedical Circuits and Systems
10. Neural Networks and Neuromorphic Engineering
11. **High-Performance Computing for AI** — the closest match to "hardware compression for disaggregated LLM inference"; this track name is a strong signal ISCAS 2027 explicitly wants AI-infrastructure hardware papers
12. Circuits and Systems for Quantum Computing
13. Beyond CMOS: Nanoelectronics and Heterogeneous Integration
14. Education in Circuits and Systems

## 6. Caveats / watch items

- The regular-paper page limit and review-blindness for 2027 are inferred from the stable 2024-2026 rule; the 2027 author instructions page did not exist as of 2026-07-14. Re-verify when it appears (typically alongside submission-site opening, ~September).
- The IEEE CASS event page (https://ieee-cas.org/event/conference/2027-ieee-international-symposium-circuits-and-systems) returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch; the deadline and dates above are from the conference's own site, which is the authoritative source anyway.
- ISCAS deadlines historically do sometimes get short extensions, but plan for the published October 13, 2026 date.
